title: Chinese grammar
about: From your very first conversation to everyday Chinese, one short lesson at a time. Each lesson gives you something you can say straight away, then the grammar that makes it work. You don't need to know any grammar: each grammar word is explained when you first need it. Chinese verbs never change, so the grammar is mostly word order and a few small words, and you can say a lot very soon. Every example is in simplified characters with its pinyin, the reading in Latin letters with the tones.

lessons.title: Say hello and who you are
lessons.summary: Greet someone, say your name and where you're from, and ask them the same: your first conversation in Chinese.
lessons.topic: {{我是…|wǒ shì…}} and {{我叫…|wǒ jiào…}}; {{你呢？|nǐ ne?}}; verbs that never change

goal.t: 你好！我叫安娜，我是美国人。
goal.r: Nǐ hǎo! Wǒ jiào Ānnà, wǒ shì Měiguórén.
goal.tr: Hi! My name is Anna, I'm American.

dialog.r: Nǐ hǎo! Wǒ jiào Wáng Míng. Nǐ ne?
dialog.tr: Hello! My name is Wang Ming. And you?

dialog.t: 你好！我叫安娜。我是美国人。
dialog.r: Nǐ hǎo! Wǒ jiào Ānnà. Wǒ shì Měiguórén.
dialog.tr: Hi! I'm Anna. I'm American.

dialog.t: 我是中国人，我是北京人。
dialog.r: Wǒ shì Zhōngguórén, wǒ shì Běijīngrén.
dialog.tr: I'm Chinese, I'm from Beijing.

dialog.r: Rènshi nǐ hěn gāoxìng!
dialog.tr: Nice to meet you!

dialog.r: Wǒ yě hěn gāoxìng!
dialog.tr: Nice to meet you too!

blocks.p: Look at the two verbs Anna uses. {{是|shì}} means “am, is, are”, and {{叫|jiào}} means “am called”. In Chinese a verb **never changes**: {{我是|wǒ shì}} “I am”, {{你是|nǐ shì}} “you are”, {{他是|tā shì}} “he is”. There are no endings to learn, ever: not for who does it, and not for when.

blocks.means: a word for an action or a state: eat, go, be, be called.
a short word that stands for a person or a thing: I, you, he, she.

blocks.p: **More than one person** is the same word with {{们|men}}: {{我们|wǒmen}} “we”, {{他们|tāmen}} “they”. {{他|tā}} “he” and {{她|tā}} “she” sound exactly the same; only the writing is different.

**Where you're from**: the country + {{人|rén}} “person”. {{美国|Měiguó}} is America, so {{美国人|Měiguórén}} is “an American”; {{中国人|Zhōngguórén}} is “a Chinese person”. And there is no word for “a”: {{我是学生。|Wǒ shì xuésheng.}} is, word for word, “I am student”.
**And you?** Put {{呢|ne}} after a word to turn the question back: {{你呢？|Nǐ ne?}} “And you?”

ex.note: word for word: “I am called David”
a set phrase: “knowing you, (I'm) very happy”

blocks.tip: The marks over the vowels are the tones, and the next lesson shows how to say them. Until then, tap an example to hear it, and copy the melody as well as the sounds.

mistakes.why: {{叫|jiào}} already means “am called”: no {{是|shì}} with it. Say {{我叫安娜。|Wǒ jiào Ānnà.}}, or {{我是安娜。|Wǒ shì Ānnà.}} “I'm Anna”.
{{美国|Měiguó}} is the country, so this says “I am America”! A person from it is {{美国人|Měiguórén}}.

practice.q: {{她|tā}} means…
practice.why: {{她|tā}} is “she” (it has {{女|nǚ}} “woman” on its left); {{他|tā}} is “he”. They sound the same.

lessons.title: Read pinyin and say the tones
lessons.summary: Read the pinyin under every example, and hear the four tones that make {{妈|mā}} “mum” and {{马|mǎ}} “horse” two different words.
lessons.topic: Characters and pinyin; the four tones and the light tone; how {{不|bù}} and {{一|yī}} change

blocks.p: Chinese is written in **characters**. Each character is one syllable with a meaning: {{人|rén}} “person”, {{好|hǎo}} “good”, {{大|dà}} “big”. A character doesn't show how it's said, so learners (and Chinese children) use **pinyin**: the same sounds in Latin letters. Every example in this course has its pinyin, and you can hide it once you know the characters.
**The tones.** Every syllable is said with a melody, its tone, shown by the mark over the vowel. The tone is part of the word, as much as its letters:

table: high and level, as if singing a note
falling, short and firm, like a firm “No!”

blocks.p: So {{买|mǎi}} is “buy” and {{卖|mài}} is “sell”. Don't worry about getting every tone right from the start: listen, copy, and people will understand you, as they understand a foreign accent in English.
**Letters that don't sound like English.** Most pinyin letters sound as you'd guess. These don't:

table: ü (after j, q, x: written u)

blocks.p: **Tones that change.** Two 3rd tones in a row: the first one rises, so {{你好|nǐ hǎo}} is said “ní hǎo” (the pinyin keeps nǐ). {{不|bù}} “not” becomes bú before a 4th tone: {{不是|bú shì}}. {{一|yī}} “one” becomes yí before a 4th tone and yì before the others: {{一个|yí ge}}, {{一起|yìqǐ}}. This course writes the changed tones of {{不|bù}} and {{一|yī}}, as Chinese textbooks do.

blocks.tip: One character, one syllable: count the syllables of the pinyin and you know how many characters there are. {{谢谢你|xièxie nǐ}} “thank you”: three.

mistakes.tr: I'd like to ask you a question.
mistakes.why: {{问|wèn}}, falling, is “ask”; said dipping, {{吻|wěn}}, it's “kiss”: “I'd like to kiss you a question”. Tones matter!

mistakes.tr: I'd like a bowl of soup.
mistakes.why: {{汤|tāng}}, high and level, is soup; {{糖|táng}}, rising, is sugar: a bowl of sugar!

practice.q: Which tone is {{是|shì}}?
practice.why: The mark falls, like the voice: shì.

practice.q: Before {{是|shì}}, {{不|bù}} is said…
practice.why: Before a 4th tone, bù becomes bú: {{不是|bú shì}}.

practice.q: How many characters are there in {{谢谢你|xièxie nǐ}}?
practice.why: One character for each syllable: xiè, xie, nǐ.

practice.q: Put the words in order.

Your turn: someone says {{谢谢！|Xièxie!}} What do you answer? Then say goodbye.

answers.r: Bú kèqi! Zàijiàn!
answers.tr: You're welcome! Goodbye!

answers.r: Bú kèqi! Míngtiān jiàn!

lessons.title: Ask yes-or-no questions
lessons.summary: Turn any sentence into a question with one small word, and answer “yes” and “no” the Chinese way.
lessons.topic: {{吗|ma}} questions; answering with the verb ({{是|shì}} / {{不是|bú shì}}); {{不|bù}} “not”; {{也|yě}} “too”

dialog.r: Nǐ shì lǎoshī ma?
dialog.tr: Are you a teacher?

dialog.r: Bú shì, wǒ shì yīshēng. Nǐ ne?
dialog.tr: No, I'm a doctor. And you?

dialog.t: 我是学生。你是北京人吗？
dialog.r: Wǒ shì xuésheng. Nǐ shì Běijīngrén ma?
dialog.tr: I'm a student. Are you from Beijing?

dialog.r: Shì, wǒ shì Běijīngrén.
dialog.tr: Yes, I'm from Beijing.

dialog.r: Wǒ péngyou yě shì Běijīngrén!
dialog.tr: My friend is from Beijing too!

blocks.p: **A question with {{吗|ma}}.** Take any sentence and put {{吗|ma}} at the end: {{你是老师。|Nǐ shì lǎoshī.}} “You're a teacher.” becomes {{你是老师吗？|Nǐ shì lǎoshī ma?}} “Are you a teacher?” Nothing else moves.

blocks.means: a small word with no meaning of its own that changes what a sentence does: {{吗|ma}} makes it a question.

blocks.p: **Yes and no.** Chinese has no one word for “yes” or “no”. You answer with the verb of the question: “Are you…?” “(I) am”, {{是|shì}}, or “(I) am not”, {{不是|bú shì}}. {{不|bù}} “not” goes right before the verb.

table: {{你是学生吗？|Nǐ shì xuésheng ma?}} Are you a student?
{{你去吗？|Nǐ qù ma?}} Are you going?
{{你叫大卫吗？|Nǐ jiào Dàwèi ma?}} Is your name David?

blocks.p: {{对|duì}} “right” is a handy “yes” when someone checks a fact. **Too** is {{也|yě}}, and it goes before the verb: {{我也是学生。|Wǒ yě shì xuésheng.}} “I'm a student too.” Never at the end, as in English.

ex.note: {{你们|nǐmen}}: talking to more than one person

blocks.tip: Your voice doesn't need to go up at the end of a {{吗|ma}} question, as it does in English: {{吗|ma}} already makes it a question.

mistakes.why: {{也|yě}} goes before the verb, never at the end: {{我也是学生。|Wǒ yě shì xuésheng.}}
{{不|bù}} goes right before the verb it denies: {{我不是老师。|Wǒ bú shì lǎoshī.}}

lines.why: Yes: {{是|shì}}, the verb of the question.
You're not American: {{不是|bú shì}}, then what you are.

lessons.title: Say how you are and what things are like
lessons.summary: “I'm busy”, “It's cold today”, “Chinese isn't hard”: describe people and things, without the word for “is”.
lessons.topic: Adjectives with {{很|hěn}} and no {{是|shì}}; {{不|bù}} + adjective; {{太…了|tài…le}}

dialog.r: Zuìjìn máng ma?
dialog.tr: Busy lately?

dialog.r: Hěn máng! Gōngzuò hěn duō. Nǐ ne?
dialog.tr: Very busy! Lots of work. And you?

dialog.r: Wǒ bù máng. Zhōngwén nán ma?
dialog.tr: I'm not busy. Is Chinese hard?

dialog.r: Bù nán! Hěn yǒu yìsi.
dialog.tr: Not hard! It's really interesting.

dialog.r: Tài hǎo le!
dialog.tr: Great!

blocks.p: **No “is” with describing words.** To say what someone or something is *like*, put the describing word straight after it, usually with {{很|hěn}}: {{我很忙。|Wǒ hěn máng.}} “I'm busy.” There is no {{是|shì}} here: {{是|shì}} joins two nouns (“I am a student”), not a person and a description.

blocks.means: a word that describes a person or a thing: big, cold, busy, happy.

blocks.p: {{很|hěn}} means “very”, but in a plain sentence it's said lightly, almost without meaning, to make the sentence sound finished: {{我很好。|Wǒ hěn hǎo.}} is just “I'm fine”. In a {{吗|ma}} question and after {{不|bù}}, there's no {{很|hěn}}:
**Too, so** is {{太|tài}} before the adjective and {{了|le}} after it: {{太贵了！|Tài guì le!}} “Too expensive!”, {{太好了！|Tài hǎo le!}} “Great!”

blocks.tip: {{你好吗？|Nǐ hǎo ma?}} “How are you?” is in every textbook, but friends more often ask {{最近怎么样？|Zuìjìn zěnmeyàng?}} “How have you been?” or {{最近忙吗？|Zuìjìn máng ma?}} “Busy lately?”

mistakes.why: No {{是|shì}} before a describing word: {{我很忙。|Wǒ hěn máng.}}
{{不|bù}} goes straight before the adjective, with no {{是|shì}} here either: {{我不忙。|Wǒ bù máng.}}

practice.q: Choose the missing word.

practice.q: A friend calls. Choose your replies.

{{不累|bú lèi}}: {{不|bù}} straight before the adjective. Then turn the question back with {{呢|ne}}.

lessons.title: Ask who, what and where
lessons.summary: “What's your name?”, “Who's she?”, “Where are you from?”: ask for information, and leave every word where it is.
lessons.topic: Question words {{什么|shénme}}, {{谁|shéi}}, {{哪|nǎ}}, {{哪儿|nǎr}}: in the place of the answer

dialog.r: Tā shì shéi?
dialog.tr: Who's she?

dialog.r: Tā shì wǒ péngyou, jiào Mǎlì.
dialog.tr: She's my friend, her name is Mary.

dialog.r: Tā shì nǎ guó rén?
dialog.tr: Where's she from?

dialog.r: Tā shì Fǎguórén.
dialog.tr: She's French.

dialog.r: Tā zuò shénme gōngzuò?
dialog.tr: What does she do?

dialog.r: Tā shì lǎoshī.
dialog.tr: She's a teacher.

blocks.p: **The question word goes where the answer goes.** English moves “what” and “who” to the front; Chinese moves nothing. Say the sentence as if you knew, and put the question word in the gap:

table: {{我叫安娜。|Wǒ jiào Ānnà.}} I'm called Anna.
{{你叫什么？|Nǐ jiào shénme?}} You're called what?
{{她是玛丽。|Tā shì Mǎlì.}} She's Mary.
{{他是美国人。|Tā shì Měiguórén.}} He's American.
{{他是哪国人？|Tā shì nǎ guó rén?}} He's which-country person?
{{这是茶。|Zhè shì chá.}} This is tea.
{{这是什么？|Zhè shì shénme?}} This is what?

blocks.means: a word that asks for a piece of information: what, who, where, how many.

blocks.p: A question word already makes a question, so there's no {{吗|ma}} with it. {{谁|shéi}} “who” is also said shuí. {{哪|nǎ}} is “which”, and {{哪儿|nǎr}} “where”: northern China says {{哪儿|nǎr}}, the south {{哪里|nǎlǐ}}, and both are right.

ex.note: the answer (“Mr Li is…”) would come first, so {{谁|shéi}} comes first

blocks.tip: A polite way to ask a name: {{您贵姓？|Nín guìxìng?}} “What's your family name?” ({{您|nín}} is a respectful “you”). In Chinese the family name comes first: {{王明|Wáng Míng}} is Mr Wang.

mistakes.why: Don't move the question word to the front: it stays where the answer goes. {{你叫什么？|Nǐ jiào shénme?}}
A question word already asks: no {{吗|ma}}.

{{英国人|Yīngguórén}} takes the place of {{哪国人|nǎ guó rén}}.
You're answering, not asking: no {{吗|ma}}.

lessons.title: Count people and things
lessons.summary: Count from one to ninety-nine, and count people and things the Chinese way, with a measure word: “three (of) friends”.
lessons.topic: Numbers; measure words and {{个|gè}}; {{两|liǎng}} for “two”; {{几|jǐ}} “how many?”

dialog.r: Huānyíng guānglín! Jǐ wèi?
dialog.tr: Welcome! How many?

dialog.r: Wǒmen sān ge rén.
dialog.tr: There are three of us.

dialog.r: Hǎo, sān wèi, zhèbiān qǐng.
dialog.tr: OK, three, this way please.

blocks.p: **Bigger numbers are built like sums.** {{十一|shíyī}} 11 is “ten one”, {{二十|èrshí}} 20 is “two ten”, {{二十五|èrshíwǔ}} 25 is “two ten five”, and so on up to {{九十九|jiǔshíjiǔ}} 99. Once you know one to ten, you know them all.

blocks.means: a word for a person, a thing or an idea: friend, apple, city.
a small word that goes between a number (or “this”, “that”) and a noun, like “cup” in “two cups of tea”. Chinese needs one every time it counts.

blocks.p: **A measure word between the number and the noun.** English says “three friends”; Chinese says “three *ge* friends”: {{三个朋友|sān ge péngyou}}. A number can't go straight before a noun. {{个|gè}} is the commonest measure word, for people and many things, and it's usually said lightly: ge.
**Two** is {{两|liǎng}} before a measure word: {{两个人|liǎng ge rén}} “two people”. {{二|èr}} is for counting (“one, two, three”) and inside longer numbers: {{十二|shí'èr}} 12, {{二十|èrshí}} 20.
**How many?** {{几|jǐ}} + measure word asks about a small number, up to about ten: {{几个人？|Jǐ ge rén?}} “How many people?” The answer goes where {{几|jǐ}} was, as with every question word.

ex.tr: How many of you are there?

blocks.tip: In a restaurant you'll hear {{几位？|Jǐ wèi?}}: {{位|wèi}} is a polite measure word for people. Answer with the number: {{三个人|sān ge rén}}, or just {{三个|sān ge}}.

mistakes.why: A number needs a measure word before the noun: {{三个朋友|sān ge péngyou}}.
Before a measure word, “two” is {{两|liǎng}}: {{两个人|liǎng ge rén}}.

practice.why: “Two ten five”: 2 × 10 + 5.

lessons.title: Point and choose: this one, that one
lessons.summary: “This book”, “that cup”, “Which one?”: point at things in a shop and pick the one you want.
lessons.topic: {{这|zhè}}, {{那|nà}}, {{哪|nǎ}} + measure word; {{本|běn}}, {{杯|bēi}}, {{张|zhāng}}, {{件|jiàn}}, {{只|zhī}}

goal.r: Zhè běn shū hěn yǒu yìsi.

dialog.r: Nà shì shénme?
dialog.tr: What's that?

dialog.r: Nà shì chábēi.
dialog.tr: Those are teacups.

dialog.r: Nǎge?
dialog.tr: Which one?

dialog.r: Zhège?
dialog.tr: This one?

dialog.r: Bú shì, nàge. Hěn piàoliang!
dialog.tr: No, that one. It's beautiful!

blocks.p: **This and that.** {{这|zhè}} is “this”, {{那|nà}} is “that”. On their own, before {{是|shì}}: {{这是茶。|Zhè shì chá.}} “This is tea.” But before a noun they need a measure word, just like a number: {{这个人|zhège rén}} “this person”, {{那个城市|nàge chéngshì}} “that city”.

**Measure words for kinds of things.** {{个|gè}} goes with many nouns, but some have a measure word of their own, chosen by the shape or kind of thing. Learn each noun together with its measure word, as one piece:

table: a cup or a glass of
{{一杯茶|yì bēi chá}} a cup of tea
{{一件衣服|yí jiàn yīfu}} a top

blocks.p: **Just “this one”.** Once everyone knows what you're talking about, drop the noun: {{这个很好。|Zhège hěn hǎo.}} “This one's good.” A number fits between too: {{这两张票|zhè liǎng zhāng piào}} “these two tickets”.

ex.r: Zhè běn shū hěn yǒu yìsi.

ex.note: this or that, then the number, then the measure word

blocks.tip: Not sure of the measure word? Use {{个|gè}}: it isn't always right, but people will understand you. And in fast speech {{这个|zhège}} and {{那个|nàge}} are often said “zhèige” and “nèige”.

mistakes.why: A number needs its measure word before the noun, even after {{这|zhè}}: {{这两本书|zhè liǎng běn shū}}.
Books have a measure word of their own: {{一本书|yì běn shū}}.

practice.q: Choose the missing word.
practice.why: Books: {{本|běn}}.

practice.q: “That cat” is…

lessons.title: Order food and drink
lessons.summary: Ask for what you want in a café or a restaurant, and say what you'd like to do: “I'll have a coffee”, “I feel like dumplings”.
lessons.topic: {{要|yào}} and {{想要|xiǎng yào}} + a thing; {{想|xiǎng}} + a verb; {{和|hé}} “and”; {{来|lái}} for ordering

dialog.r: Nǐ hǎo! Yào shénme?
dialog.tr: Hi! What would you like?

dialog.t: 我要一杯咖啡和一块蛋糕。

blocks.p: **{{要|yào}}: I want, I'll have.** {{要|yào}} + the thing is how you order and ask for things in a shop, a café or a taxi. It sounds normal and polite, not pushy, especially with {{谢谢|xièxie}}: {{我要这个，谢谢。|Wǒ yào zhège, xièxie.}} “I'll have this one, thanks.”

**{{想|xiǎng}} + a verb: I'd like to.** {{想|xiǎng}} “would like to, feel like” goes before what you'd like to do: {{我想喝茶。|Wǒ xiǎng hē chá.}} “I'd like some tea” (“I'd like to drink tea”). {{想要|xiǎng yào}} + a thing is a softer “I'd like”.

table: {{我要一杯茶。|Wǒ yào yì bēi chá.}}
{{我想要一杯茶。|Wǒ xiǎng yào yì bēi chá.}}

blocks.p: **And** between two things is {{和|hé}}: {{一杯咖啡和一块蛋糕|yì bēi kāfēi hé yí kuài dàngāo}}. It joins nouns only; a later lesson shows how to join two sentences. **Ordering like a local**: {{来|lái}} “come” + the dish: {{来一碗面！|Lái yì wǎn miàn!}} “A bowl of noodles!”

blocks.tip: Waiters often ask {{还要别的吗？|Hái yào bié de ma?}} “Anything else?”; {{不要了，谢谢。|Bú yào le, xièxie.}} means “That's all, thanks.” To call a waiter, say {{服务员！|Fúwùyuán!}}

A number needs a measure word: {{一杯咖啡|yì bēi kāfēi}}.

lessons.title: Ask how much it costs
lessons.summary: Ask the price, understand the answer, and haggle a little: “How much is this?” “Thirty-five yuan.” “Too expensive!”
lessons.topic: {{多少钱？|duōshao qián?}}; money: {{块|kuài}} and {{毛|máo}}; hundreds and thousands; a price needs no {{是|shì}}

dialog.r: Zhège duōshao qián?
dialog.tr: How much is this?

dialog.tr: Thirty-five yuan.

blocks.p: **Asking the price.** {{多少钱？|Duōshao qián?}} is “how much money?”, and it goes after the thing: {{这个多少钱？|Zhège duōshao qián?}}, {{这本书多少钱？|Zhè běn shū duōshao qián?}} {{多少|duōshao}} “how much, how many” is for any number, big or small; {{几|jǐ}} is only for small ones.
**No “is” before a price.** The answer is just the thing and the price, side by side: {{这个三十块。|Zhège sānshí kuài.}} “This one is thirty yuan.” As with adjectives, there's no {{是|shì}}.

**The money.** China's money is the yuan: {{元|yuán}} on price tags, {{块|kuài}} when people speak. A tenth of a yuan is {{毛|máo}}: {{五块五|wǔ kuài wǔ}} is 5.50, “five kuai five”. People often add {{钱|qián}} “money”: {{十块钱|shí kuài qián}} “ten yuan”.

table: two hundred zero eight: {{零|líng}} fills a gap

blocks.p: Before {{百|bǎi}} and {{千|qiān}}, “two” is often {{两|liǎng}} too: {{两百|liǎngbǎi}} 200, {{两千|liǎngqiān}} 2,000.

ex.tr: How much are the apples per jin?
ex.note: a {{斤|jīn}} is half a kilo, the usual weight at markets

ex.r: Tài guì le! Piányi yìdiǎnr ba.

lessons.title: Say whose it is
lessons.summary: “My phone”, “the teacher's book”, “Whose is this?”: say who things belong to.
lessons.topic: {{的|de}}: {{我的|wǒ de}}, {{老师的|lǎoshī de}}, {{谁的|shéi de}}; {{我妈妈|wǒ māma}} without {{的|de}}

dialog.r: Zhè shì shéi de shū?
dialog.tr: Whose book is this?

dialog.r: Bú shì wǒ de. Shì Ānnà de ma?
dialog.tr: It's not mine. Is it Anna's?

dialog.r: Duì, shì wǒ de! Xièxie lǎoshī!
dialog.tr: Yes, it's mine! Thank you!

dialog.r: Zhège shǒujī ne?
dialog.tr: And this phone?

dialog.r: Nà shì wǒ de.
dialog.tr: That's mine.

blocks.p: **{{的|de}} is like 's.** Put {{的|de}} after the owner, then the thing: {{老师的书|lǎoshī de shū}} “the teacher's book”, {{我的手机|wǒ de shǒujī}} “my phone” (“I's phone”). The owner always comes first, as with 's in English.

**Mine, yours.** Leave the thing out, and {{我的|wǒ de}} means “mine”: {{这是我的。|Zhè shì wǒ de.}} “This is mine.” **Whose?** is {{谁的|shéi de}}, in the owner's place: {{这是谁的书？|Zhè shì shéi de shū?}} “Whose book is this?”

**Close people: no {{的|de}}.** With family, friends, and places you belong to (your home, school or company), {{的|de}} is usually left out: {{我妈妈|wǒ māma}} “my mum”, {{我朋友|wǒ péngyou}} “my friend”, {{我们公司|wǒmen gōngsī}} “our company”. With things, keep it: {{我的书|wǒ de shū}}.

ex.r: Wǒ de Zhōngwén lǎoshī hěn hǎo.
Zhè bēi kāfēi shì nǐ de ma?

blocks.tip: {{的|de}} is the commonest character in Chinese. Owners are its first job; later lessons show it joining descriptions to nouns too.

mistakes.why: Things take {{的|de}}: {{我的书|wǒ de shū}}. Only close people and places leave it out ({{我妈妈|wǒ māma}}).
The owner first, then {{的|de}}, then the thing: {{老师的书|lǎoshī de shū}}. {{书的老师|shū de lǎoshī}} would be “the book's teacher”.

lessons.title: Talk about your family
lessons.summary: Say who's in your family and how old they are, and what you have and don't have: “I have an older brother and a younger sister.”
lessons.topic: {{有|yǒu}} “have” and {{没有|méiyǒu}} (never {{不有|bù yǒu}}); {{几口人|jǐ kǒu rén}}; ages without {{是|shì}}; {{都|dōu}} “all”

goal.t: 我有一个哥哥和一个妹妹。
goal.r: Wǒ yǒu yí ge gēge hé yí ge mèimei.
goal.tr: I have an older brother and a younger sister.

dialog.r: Nǐ jiā yǒu jǐ kǒu rén?
dialog.tr: How many people are there in your family?

dialog.t: 四口人：爸爸、妈妈、姐姐和我。
dialog.r: Sì kǒu rén: bàba, māma, jiějie hé wǒ.
dialog.tr: Four: my dad, my mum, my older sister and me.

dialog.r: Nǐ jiějie duō dà?
dialog.tr: How old is your sister?

dialog.t: 她二十六岁。你有兄弟姐妹吗？
dialog.r: Tā èrshíliù suì. Nǐ yǒu xiōngdì jiěmèi ma?
dialog.tr: She's twenty-six. Do you have any brothers or sisters?

dialog.r: Méiyǒu, wǒ shì dúshēngzǐ.
dialog.tr: No, I'm an only child.

blocks.p: **{{有|yǒu}} “have”.** {{我有一个哥哥。|Wǒ yǒu yí ge gēge.}} “I have an older brother.” Like every verb, it never changes: {{他有|tā yǒu}} “he has”. Ask with {{吗|ma}}: {{你有孩子吗？|Nǐ yǒu háizi ma?}} “Do you have children?”

**Not have: {{没有|méiyǒu}}.** {{有|yǒu}} is the one verb that never takes {{不|bù}}: “don't have” is always {{没有|méiyǒu}}, or just {{没|méi}}: {{我没有车。|Wǒ méiyǒu chē.}} “I don't have a car.” The short answer “no” to {{你有…吗？|Nǐ yǒu… ma?}} is {{没有。|Méiyǒu.}}

Chinese has no plain word for “brother” or “sister”: you always say whether they're older or younger. **How many in your family?** {{你家有几口人？|Nǐ jiā yǒu jǐ kǒu rén?}}: {{口|kǒu}} “mouth” is the measure word for the people in a family.

**Ages without {{是|shì}}.** Like a price, an age goes straight after the person, with {{岁|suì}} “years old”: {{我三十岁。|Wǒ sānshí suì.}} “I'm thirty.” Ask an adult {{你多大？|Nǐ duō dà?}} “How old are you?” and a child {{你几岁？|Nǐ jǐ suì?}}
**All, both** is {{都|dōu}}, and it goes before the verb, like {{也|yě}}: {{我们都是学生。|Wǒmen dōu shì xuésheng.}} “We're all students.”

ex.tr: I don't have any brothers or sisters.

ex.r: Wǒ bàba māma dōu shì lǎoshī.
ex.tr: My mum and dad are both teachers.

lessons.title: Say where things are
lessons.summary: “Where's my phone?” “On the table.” Say where people and things are, and ask where they are.
lessons.topic: {{在|zài}} + a place; {{上|shang}}, {{里|li}}, {{下面|xiàmiàn}}, {{旁边|pángbiān}}, {{前面|qiánmiàn}}, {{后面|hòumiàn}} after the noun

dialog.r: Mā, wǒ de shǒujī zài nǎr?
dialog.tr: Mum, where's my phone?

blocks.p: **{{在|zài}}: to be in a place.** The person or thing, then {{在|zài}}, then the place: {{我在家。|Wǒ zài jiā.}} “I'm at home.” {{老师在学校。|Lǎoshī zài xuéxiào.}} “The teacher is at school.” Here {{在|zài}} is the verb, so “not” is {{不在|bú zài}}: {{他不在。|Tā bú zài.}} “He isn't here.”
**On, in, under: after the noun.** English says “on the table”; Chinese says “table on”: {{桌子上|zhuōzi shang}}. The place word always comes after the thing:
**Where?** is {{哪儿|nǎr}}, in the place of the answer as always: {{你在哪儿？|Nǐ zài nǎr?}} “Where are you?” **Here** is {{这儿|zhèr}} and **there** is {{那儿|nàr}}; in the south, {{这里|zhèlǐ}} and {{那里|nàlǐ}}.

ex.tr: The keys are on the table.
The cat is under the chair.
The bank is next to the supermarket.

blocks.tip: Cities and countries need no place word: {{我在北京。|Wǒ zài Běijīng.}} “I'm in Beijing.” Things you can be in, on or under do: {{在房间里|zài fángjiān li}} “in the room”.

mistakes.why: The place word goes after the noun: {{桌子上|zhuōzi shang}}, “table on”.
{{在|zài}} is already the verb “to be (somewhere)”: no {{是|shì}} needed. {{我在家。|Wǒ zài jiā.}}

lessons.title: Say what there is
lessons.summary: “There's a café near here”, “Is there a bank nearby?”, “There's no one in the room”: say what there is in a place.
lessons.topic: The place + {{有|yǒu}} + the thing; {{没有|méiyǒu}}; {{有|yǒu}} for something new, {{在|zài}} for something known

dialog.r: Qǐngwèn, fùjìn yǒu yínháng ma?
dialog.tr: Excuse me, is there a bank near here?

dialog.t: 有。前面有一个中国银行。
dialog.r: Yǒu. Qiánmiàn yǒu yí ge Zhōngguó Yínháng.
dialog.tr: Yes. There's a Bank of China up ahead.

dialog.r: Fùjìn yǒu dìtiězhàn ma?
dialog.tr: Is there a subway station nearby?

dialog.r: Méiyǒu, dìtiězhàn hěn yuǎn.
dialog.tr: No, the subway station is far.

dialog.r: Hǎo, xièxie!
dialog.tr: OK, thanks!

blocks.p: **There is: the place, then {{有|yǒu}}.** Chinese uses the same {{有|yǒu}} as “have”: the place “has” the thing. So the place comes first: {{附近有一个银行。|Fùjìn yǒu yí ge yínháng.}} “There's a bank nearby” (“nearby has a bank”). {{房间里有两张床。|Fángjiān li yǒu liǎng zhāng chuáng.}} “There are two beds in the room.”
**There isn't** is {{没有|méiyǒu}}: {{冰箱里没有牛奶。|Bīngxiāng li méiyǒu niúnǎi.}} “There's no milk in the fridge.” Ask with {{吗|ma}}, and answer {{有|yǒu}} or {{没有|méiyǒu}}.

**{{有|yǒu}} or {{在|zài}}?** Both are about places, but they start from different ends. {{有|yǒu}} brings in something new: “There's a bank up ahead.” {{在|zài}} says where something already known is: “The bank is up ahead.”

table: {{前面有一个银行。|Qiánmiàn yǒu yí ge yínháng.}}

ex.r: Zhuōzi shang yǒu yì běn shū.
ex.tr: There's a book on the table.
There's no one in the classroom.

ex.r: Wǒ jiā pángbiān yǒu yí ge gōngyuán.
ex.tr: There's a park next to my home.

ex.r: Běijīng yǒu hěn duō hǎochī de.
ex.tr: There's lots of good food in Beijing.

blocks.tip: {{请问|qǐngwèn}} “may I ask” is the polite way to start a question to a stranger, like “Excuse me”: {{请问，洗手间在哪儿？|Qǐngwèn, xǐshǒujiān zài nǎr?}} “Excuse me, where's the restroom?”

lessons.title: Say when: days, dates and times
lessons.summary: Say what day and time it is, give dates, and put “when” in its Chinese place: “I'm going to Beijing tomorrow.”
lessons.topic: {{今天|jīntiān}}, {{星期一|xīngqīyī}}, {{几月几号|jǐ yuè jǐ hào}}, {{几点|jǐ diǎn}}; from big to small; the time before the verb

dialog.r: Jīntiān xīngqī jǐ?
dialog.tr: What day is it today?

dialog.r: Jīntiān xīngqīwǔ.
dialog.tr: It's Friday.

dialog.r: Nǐ jǐ diǎn shàngkè?
dialog.tr: What time is your class?

dialog.r: Wǒ xiàwǔ liǎng diǎn shàngkè.
dialog.tr: My class is at two in the afternoon.

dialog.r: Wǒmen wǎnshang qī diǎn jiàn, hǎo ma?
dialog.tr: Let's meet at seven this evening, OK?

dialog.r: Hǎo! Wǎnshang jiàn!
dialog.tr: OK! See you tonight!

blocks.p: **The days of the week are numbered.** {{星期|xīngqī}} “week” + a number: {{星期一|xīngqīyī}} Monday (“week one”), {{星期二|xīngqī'èr}} Tuesday, and so on to {{星期六|xīngqīliù}} Saturday. Sunday is {{星期天|xīngqītiān}}. “What day?” is {{星期几？|xīngqī jǐ?}}

**Dates go from big to small**: year, month, day. Months are numbered too: {{一月|yīyuè}} January, {{十月|shíyuè}} October. The day is {{号|hào}}: {{十月二十四号|shíyuè èrshísì hào}} “24 October”. A year is read digit by digit: {{二〇二六年|èr líng èr liù nián}} 2026.

**Clock times**: {{点|diǎn}} “o'clock”, {{半|bàn}} “half past”, {{分|fēn}} “minutes”: {{三点|sān diǎn}} 3:00, {{三点半|sān diǎn bàn}} 3:30, {{三点十分|sān diǎn shí fēn}} 3:10. Two o'clock is {{两点|liǎng diǎn}}. Big to small again: {{明天下午三点|míngtiān xiàwǔ sān diǎn}} “at three tomorrow afternoon”.

**When goes before the verb.** English puts “tomorrow” at the end; Chinese puts the time after the person, or right at the start, and never after the verb: {{我明天去北京。|Wǒ míngtiān qù Běijīng.}} or {{明天我去北京。|Míngtiān wǒ qù Běijīng.}} Like prices and ages, days and times need no {{是|shì}}: {{今天星期五。|Jīntiān xīngqīwǔ.}} (With a longer subject people often add it: {{我的生日是三月十五号。|Wǒ de shēngrì shì sānyuè shíwǔ hào.}} Both are fine.)

ex.tr: He goes to bed at ten at night.

blocks.tip: Phone numbers, room numbers and years are read digit by digit, and 1 is often said {{幺|yāo}} so it can't be mistaken for 7: {{房间幺零八|fángjiān yāo líng bā}} “room 108”.

lessons.title: Say where you do things
lessons.summary: “I work in a bank”, “We're eating at home”: say where you do things, in the order Chinese always uses: who, when, where, what.
lessons.topic: {{在|zài}} + a place + a verb; the order: who + when + where + does what

dialog.r: Nǐ zài nǎr gōngzuò?
dialog.tr: Where do you work?

dialog.t: 我在一家公司工作。你呢？
dialog.r: Wǒ zài yì jiā gōngsī gōngzuò. Nǐ ne?
dialog.tr: I work for a company. And you?

dialog.t: 我在医院工作，我是护士。
dialog.r: Wǒ zài yīyuàn gōngzuò, wǒ shì hùshi.
dialog.tr: I work in a hospital, I'm a nurse.

dialog.r: Nǐ měitiān zài yīyuàn chīfàn ma?
dialog.tr: Do you eat at the hospital every day?

dialog.r: Bù, wǒ zhōngwǔ zài jiā chīfàn.
dialog.tr: No, I eat at home at lunchtime.

blocks.p: **Where you do it goes before the verb.** In the last lessons {{在|zài}} was the verb (“to be at”). Put an action after the place, and {{在|zài}} becomes “at, in”: {{我在银行工作。|Wǒ zài yínháng gōngzuò.}} “I work in a bank” (“I at bank work”). The place always comes before the action, never after it as in English.

blocks.means: the person or thing a sentence is about, usually the one doing something: “I” in “I drink tea”.
the person or thing the action is done to: “tea” in “I drink tea”.

blocks.p: **The order of a Chinese sentence**: who (the subject), when, where, the verb, then what (the object).

The time can also go first, before the person: {{明天我在家看书。|Míngtiān wǒ zài jiā kàn shū.}} But the place stays just before the verb. **Not** goes before the place: {{我不在家吃饭。|Wǒ bú zài jiā chīfàn.}} “I don't eat at home.”

ex.tr: We're eating out at a restaurant today.

ex.r: Wǒ míngtiān zài jiā kàn shū.
Tā měitiān zài gōngsī chī wǔfàn.
ex.tr: He has lunch at the office every day.

blocks.tip: One common exception: with {{住|zhù}} “live”, the place usually comes after: {{我住在上海。|Wǒ zhù zài Shànghǎi.}} “I live in Shanghai.” And {{家|jiā}} is also the measure word for companies, shops and restaurants: {{一家公司|yì jiā gōngsī}}.

lessons.title: Describe your day
lessons.summary: “I take the subway to work”, “I'm going to the supermarket to buy food”, “First I have a coffee, then…”: put actions in a row.
lessons.topic: Verbs in a row: {{去|qù}} + place + verb, {{坐|zuò}} + vehicle + {{去|qù}}; {{怎么|zěnme}} “how”; {{先…然后…|xiān… ránhòu…}}

goal.r: Wǒ měitiān zuò dìtiě qù shàngbān.
goal.tr: I take the subway to work every day.

dialog.r: Nǐ měitiān zěnme qù shàngbān?
dialog.tr: How do you get to work every day?

dialog.r: Wǒ zuò dìtiě qù. Nǐ ne?
dialog.tr: I take the subway. And you?

dialog.tr: I go by bike.

dialog.t: 我先去超市买菜，然后回家做饭。

dialog.tr: First I go to the supermarket to buy food, then I go home and cook.

blocks.p: **Verbs in a row.** Chinese strings actions together in the order they happen, with no “to” or “and” between them: {{我去超市买东西。|Wǒ qù chāoshì mǎi dōngxi.}} “I'm going to the supermarket to buy some things” (“I go supermarket buy things”). The first action often says how or where; the next one says what for.

table: {{去超市买东西|qù chāoshì mǎi dōngxi}}
go to the supermarket to buy things
{{来中国学中文|lái Zhōngguó xué Zhōngwén}}

blocks.p: **How?** {{怎么|zěnme}} + verb asks how something is done: {{你怎么去？|Nǐ zěnme qù?}} “How are you getting there?” **First…, then…** is {{先|xiān}}…, {{然后|ránhòu}}…: {{先|xiān}} goes before the first verb, and {{然后|ránhòu}} starts the next part.

ex.r: Wǒ měitiān zuò dìtiě qù shàngbān.
ex.tr: I take the subway to work every day.
I'm going to the supermarket to buy some things.
He's come to China to study Chinese.

blocks.tip: In China people pay for almost everything with their phones, {{用手机付钱|yòng shǒujī fù qián}}, by scanning a code: {{扫码|sǎo mǎ}}.

lessons.title: Say what you like
lessons.summary: “I really like Chinese food”, “I love watching films”, “Tea or coffee?”: say what you like and don't like, and ask people to choose.
lessons.topic: {{喜欢|xǐhuan}} + a thing or a verb; {{爱|ài}}; {{最喜欢|zuì xǐhuan}}; {{还是|háishi}} “or” in questions

dialog.t: 你喜欢喝茶还是喝咖啡？
dialog.r: Nǐ xǐhuan hē chá háishi hē kāfēi?
dialog.tr: Do you like tea or coffee?

blocks.p: **{{喜欢|xǐhuan}} + a thing or an action.** {{我喜欢猫。|Wǒ xǐhuan māo.}} “I like cats.” {{我喜欢看书。|Wǒ xǐhuan kàn shū.}} “I like reading.” The action goes straight after {{喜欢|xǐhuan}}, with no “-ing” or “to”. {{很|hěn}} before it means “really”: {{我很喜欢|wǒ hěn xǐhuan}}. {{爱|ài}} “love” works the same way: {{我爱吃饺子。|Wǒ ài chī jiǎozi.}} “I love dumplings.”
**Not**: {{不喜欢|bù xǐhuan}}. **Favourite**: {{最喜欢|zuì xǐhuan}} “like most”: {{我最喜欢夏天。|Wǒ zuì xǐhuan xiàtiān.}} “Summer is my favourite season.”

**Tea or coffee?** In a question, “or” is {{还是|háishi}}, between the two choices: {{你喜欢茶还是咖啡？|Nǐ xǐhuan chá háishi kāfēi?}} There's no {{吗|ma}}: {{还是|háishi}} already asks. (In a statement, “or” is another word, for a later lesson.)

lessons.topic: {{会|huì}} (know how to), {{能|néng}} (be able to), {{可以|kěyǐ}} (be allowed to)

goal.tr: I can speak a little Chinese.

dialog.r: Nǐ huì shuō Zhōngwén ma?
dialog.tr: Can you speak Chinese?

dialog.r: Wǒ huì shuō yìdiǎnr.
dialog.tr: I can speak a little.

dialog.t: 很好！明天你能来我家吃饭吗？
dialog.r: Hěn hǎo! Míngtiān nǐ néng lái wǒ jiā chīfàn ma?
dialog.tr: Great! Can you come to my place for dinner tomorrow?

dialog.t: 明天我不能去，我要工作。星期六可以吗？
dialog.r: Míngtiān wǒ bù néng qù, wǒ yào gōngzuò. Xīngqīliù kěyǐ ma?
dialog.tr: I can't come tomorrow, I have to work. Is Saturday OK?

dialog.r: Kěyǐ!
dialog.tr: Sure!

blocks.p: English has one “can”; Chinese has three, for three different meanings. Each one goes before the verb, like {{想|xiǎng}}.

blocks.means: a verb that goes before another verb and adds an idea such as “can”, “want to” or “must”: {{会|huì}}, {{能|néng}}, {{想|xiǎng}}.

table: know how to: a skill you learned
{{我会游泳。|Wǒ huì yóuyǒng.}} I can swim.
be able to: time, health, the situation
{{我今天不能去。|Wǒ jīntiān bù néng qù.}} I can't go today.
{{这儿可以拍照吗？|Zhèr kěyǐ pāizhào ma?}} Can I take photos here?

blocks.p: So “Can you drive?” is {{你会开车吗？|Nǐ huì kāichē ma?}} (do you know how?), but “Can you drive me tomorrow?” is {{你明天能开车送我吗？|Nǐ míngtiān néng kāichē sòng wǒ ma?}} (are you able to?). To ask permission, {{可以|kěyǐ}} is the usual word: {{我可以坐这儿吗？|Wǒ kěyǐ zuò zhèr ma?}} “Can I sit here?”
**Answer with the word itself**: {{会|huì}} / {{不会|bú huì}}, {{能|néng}} / {{不能|bù néng}}, {{可以|kěyǐ}} / {{不可以|bù kěyǐ}}, or more gently {{不行|bù xíng}} “no, that won't work”.

ex.tr: I can speak a little Chinese.

ex.r: Nǐ huì zuò Zhōngguó cài ma?
Wǒ kěyǐ yòng nǐ de shǒujī ma?

blocks.tip: With languages you can drop the verb: {{我会中文|wǒ huì Zhōngwén}} “I speak Chinese”. And when someone praises your Chinese, the modest answer is {{哪里哪里！|Nǎlǐ nǎlǐ!}} “Oh, not at all!”

mistakes.why: {{会|huì}} goes before the verb, like {{想|xiǎng}}: {{我会游泳。|Wǒ huì yóuyǒng.}}

mistakes.wrong: 我明天不会来，我要工作。
mistakes.right: 我明天不能来，我要工作。
mistakes.tr: I can't come tomorrow, I have to work.
mistakes.why: You haven't forgotten how to come: work stops you, so {{不能|bù néng}}. ({{不会来|bú huì lái}} sounds like “I won't come”.)

lessons.title: Make plans and suggestions
lessons.summary: “I'm going to see my parents this weekend”, “Let's go together!”, “How about Sunday?”: talk about plans and suggest things.
lessons.topic: {{要|yào}}, {{想|xiǎng}}, {{打算|dǎsuàn}} + a verb; {{吧|ba}} for “let's”; {{…怎么样？|…zěnmeyàng?}}

goal.t: 周末我们一起去爬山吧！
goal.r: Zhōumò wǒmen yìqǐ qù pá shān ba!
goal.tr: Let's go hiking together this weekend!

dialog.t: 这个周末你打算做什么？
dialog.r: Zhège zhōumò nǐ dǎsuàn zuò shénme?
dialog.tr: What are you planning to do this weekend?

dialog.t: 星期六我要去看我爸爸妈妈。星期天没事。
dialog.r: Xīngqīliù wǒ yào qù kàn wǒ bàba māma. Xīngqītiān méi shì.
dialog.tr: On Saturday I'm going to see my parents. On Sunday I'm free.

dialog.t: 星期天我们一起去爬山吧！
dialog.r: Xīngqītiān wǒmen yìqǐ qù pá shān ba!
dialog.tr: Let's go hiking together on Sunday!

dialog.r: Hǎo a! Jǐ diǎn?
dialog.tr: Sure! What time?

dialog.r: Zǎoshang bā diǎn, zěnmeyàng?
dialog.tr: Eight in the morning, how about that?

dialog.r: Tài zǎo le! Jiǔ diǎn ba.
dialog.tr: Too early! Let's say nine.

blocks.p: **No future tense.** A time word does the job: {{明天我去上海。|Míngtiān wǒ qù Shànghǎi.}} “I'm going to Shanghai tomorrow.” To make the plan clear, add a helping verb before the action:

table: will, is going to: a firm plan
{{我明天要去上海。|Wǒ míngtiān yào qù Shànghǎi.}}
{{我打算明年去上海。|Wǒ dǎsuàn míngnián qù Shànghǎi.}}

blocks.p: **Let's…** Put {{吧|ba}} at the end of a sentence with {{我们|wǒmen}}: {{我们走吧！|Wǒmen zǒu ba!}} “Let's go!” {{吧|ba}} softens any suggestion: {{九点吧。|Jiǔ diǎn ba.}} “Let's say nine.” {{一起|yìqǐ}} “together” goes before the verb.

**How about…?** Put {{怎么样？|zěnmeyàng?}} after your idea: {{星期天怎么样？|Xīngqītiān zěnmeyàng?}} “How about Sunday?” Answer {{好啊！|Hǎo a!}} “Sure!”, {{好的。|Hǎo de.}} “OK.”, or {{不行。|Bù xíng.}} “That doesn't work.”

ex.r: Zhōumò wǒ yào qù kàn wǒ bàba māma.

lessons.title: Ask politely
lessons.summary: “Could you say that again?”, “Can I have a look?”, “Do you have a bigger one?”: ask for help and permission, politely.
lessons.topic: {{请|qǐng}} + a verb; {{可以…吗？|kěyǐ… ma?}}; A-not-A questions ({{能不能|néng bu néng}}, {{有没有|yǒu méiyǒu}}); {{一下|yíxià}} and {{看看|kànkan}}

goal.r: Qǐng nǐ zài shuō yí biàn, hǎo ma?
goal.tr: Could you say that again, please?

dialog.t: 你好，我可以看看这件衣服吗？
dialog.r: Nǐ hǎo, wǒ kěyǐ kànkan zhè jiàn yīfu ma?
dialog.tr: Hello, could I have a look at this top?

dialog.r: Kěyǐ, nǐ shì yíxià ba.
dialog.tr: Sure, try it on.

dialog.r: Yǒu méiyǒu dà yìdiǎnr de?
dialog.tr: Do you have a slightly bigger one?

dialog.r: Yǒu, qǐng děng yíxià.
dialog.tr: Yes, just a moment please.

dialog.r: Néng bu néng piányi yìdiǎnr?
dialog.tr: Could you make it a bit cheaper?

dialog.r: Bù hǎoyìsi, bù néng.
dialog.tr: Sorry, I can't.

blocks.p: **{{请|qǐng}} “please”** goes before the verb, at the start of a request: {{请进！|Qǐng jìn!}} “Please come in!”, {{请坐。|Qǐng zuò.}} “Please sit down.” Add {{好吗？|hǎo ma?}} at the end for a gentle “OK?”.

**A-not-A questions.** Instead of {{吗|ma}}, you can ask with the verb, then {{不|bù}} and the verb again: {{你去不去？|Nǐ qù bu qù?}} “Are you going (or not)?” The {{不|bu}} in the middle is said lightly. With {{有|yǒu}} it's {{有没有|yǒu méiyǒu}}. Never add {{吗|ma}} to these: they're already questions.

table: {{能便宜一点儿吗？|Néng piányi yìdiǎnr ma?}}
{{能不能便宜一点儿？|Néng bu néng piányi yìdiǎnr?}}
Do you have a big one?

blocks.p: **Just a little: {{一下|yíxià}} and doubled verbs.** After a verb, {{一下|yíxià}} “once, a moment” makes a request lighter: {{等一下|děng yíxià}} “wait a moment”, {{看一下|kàn yíxià}} “take a look”. Saying a short verb twice does the same: {{看看|kànkan}}, {{试试|shìshi}} “give it a try”.

ex.tr: Could you say that again, please?

ex.r: Nǐ néng bu néng bāng wǒ yíxià?

{{再|zài}} “again” goes before the verb: {{请再说一遍。|Qǐng zài shuō yí biàn.}}

lessons.title: Say what you did
lessons.summary: “I bought three books”, “Have you eaten?”, “I didn't go”: talk about things that happened, with {{了|le}} and {{没|méi}}.
lessons.topic: Verb + {{了|le}} for something done; {{没|méi}} + verb for “didn't” (with no {{了|le}}); {{…了吗？|…le ma?}}

goal.r: Wǒ zuótiān mǎi le sān běn shū.

dialog.r: Zhōumò nǐ zuò shénme le?
dialog.tr: What did you do at the weekend?

dialog.r: Wǒ qù le Chángchéng.
dialog.tr: I went to the Great Wall.

dialog.r: Zhēn de? Nǐ pāizhào le ma?
dialog.tr: Really? Did you take photos?

dialog.r: Pāi le hěn duō! Nǐ ne?
dialog.tr: Loads! And you?

dialog.t: 我没出去，我在家看了两部电影。
dialog.r: Wǒ méi chūqù, wǒ zài jiā kàn le liǎng bù diànyǐng.
dialog.tr: I didn't go out, I watched two films at home.

blocks.p: **Done: verb + {{了|le}}.** Chinese verbs have no past tense, but {{了|le}} right after a verb shows that the action is done, finished: {{我买了一本书。|Wǒ mǎi le yì běn shū.}} “I bought a book.” Time words say when: {{昨天|zuótiān}}, {{上个星期|shàng ge xīngqī}} “last week”.

blocks.means: how a language shows whether an action is done, going on, or something you've done before, rather than when it happens. Chinese shows aspect with small words such as {{了|le}}, {{在|zài}} and {{过|guo}}.

blocks.p: {{了|le}} isn't a past tense: it marks a finished event, especially one with a number or a detail (“bought *three* books”, “watched *two* films”). What was simply true in the past, or happened regularly, takes no {{了|le}}: {{我以前在北京工作。|Wǒ yǐqián zài Běijīng gōngzuò.}} “I used to work in Beijing.”

**Didn't: {{没|méi}} before the verb, and no {{了|le}}.** {{我没去。|Wǒ méi qù.}} “I didn't go.” {{不|bù}} is for now, the future and habits (“I don't go, I won't go”); {{没|méi}} (or {{没有|méiyǒu}}) is for what didn't happen.

table: I didn't eat. / I haven't eaten.

ex.r: Wǒ zuótiān mǎi le sān běn shū.
Wǒmen chī le hěn duō jiǎozi.

ex.tr: I didn't go to work yesterday.

blocks.tip: Around lunch or dinner time, {{你吃饭了吗？|Nǐ chīfàn le ma?}} is often just a friendly “Hi!” Answer {{吃了，你呢？|Chī le, nǐ ne?}}, even if you're starving!

mistakes.tr: I didn't go to work yesterday.
mistakes.why: Something that didn't happen takes {{没|méi}}, not {{不|bù}}: {{我昨天没去上班。|Wǒ zuótiān méi qù shàngbān.}}

lessons.title: Say what has changed
lessons.summary: “It's started raining!”, “I'm hungry now”, “I don't smoke any more”: put {{了|le}} at the end of a sentence for something new.
lessons.topic: {{了|le}} at the end: a new situation ({{下雨了|xiàyǔ le}}, {{我饿了|wǒ è le}}); {{不…了|bù… le}} “not any more”

dialog.r: Xiàyǔ le! Nǐ dài sǎn le ma?
dialog.tr: It's raining! Did you take an umbrella?

dialog.t: 带了。妈，我饿了，有什么吃的？
dialog.r: Dài le. Mā, wǒ è le, yǒu shénme chī de?
dialog.tr: Yes. Mum, I'm hungry, is there anything to eat?

dialog.r: Fàn hǎo le, lái chī ba!
dialog.tr: Dinner's ready, come and eat!

dialog.r: Tài hǎo le!
dialog.tr: Great!

blocks.p: **{{了|le}} at the end: something new.** After a whole sentence, {{了|le}} says the situation has changed: it wasn't so before. {{下雨了。|Xiàyǔ le.}} “It's raining (now).” {{我饿了。|Wǒ è le.}} “I'm hungry (now).” {{他二十岁了。|Tā èrshí suì le.}} “He's twenty now.” English often needs “now”, “has got” or “has started” to say the same.
**Not any more: {{不…了|bù… le}}.** {{我不抽烟了。|Wǒ bù chōuyān le.}} “I don't smoke any more.” {{我不去了。|Wǒ bú qù le.}} “I'm not going after all.” It's also how you change your mind.

table: {{我饿了。|Wǒ è le.}} I've got hungry, I'm hungry now.
{{我不喝酒。|Wǒ bù hē jiǔ.}} I don't drink.
{{我不喝酒了。|Wǒ bù hē jiǔ le.}} I don't drink any more.
{{天黑了。|Tiān hēi le.}} It's got dark.

blocks.p: This {{了|le}} and the {{了|le}} after a verb look the same but do different jobs: after the verb, “done”; at the end, “new”. Often one {{了|le}} at the end does both: {{我吃饭了。|Wǒ chīfàn le.}} “I've eaten.” An adjective with {{了|le}} needs no {{很|hěn}}: {{我累了。|Wǒ lèi le.}}

ex.tr: How old is your daughter now?

ex.r: Wǒ bú qù le, tài lèi le.
ex.tr: I'm not going after all, I'm too tired.
It's autumn now, it's got cold.

blocks.tip: {{好了|hǎo le}} means “it's ready, it's done”: {{饭好了！|Fàn hǎo le!}} “Dinner's ready!” And {{你怎么了？|Nǐ zěnme le?}} “What's happened to you?” is how you ask what's wrong.

mistakes.why: A habit you've stopped is {{不|bù}}…{{了|le}}: {{我不抽烟了。|Wǒ bù chōuyān le.}} {{没|méi}} is for what didn't happen.
Ages still need no {{是|shì}}: {{他二十岁了。|Tā èrshí suì le.}}

practice.q: Choose the missing word.
practice.why: Something new: {{了|le}} at the end.

practice.q: {{我不喝咖啡了。|Wǒ bù hē kāfēi le.}} means…
options: I don't drink coffee any more.
practice.why: {{不|bù}}…{{了|le}}: something you've stopped doing.

lessons.title: Say what you're doing right now
lessons.summary: “I'm cooking”, “What are you up to?”, “She's on the phone”: talk about what's going on at this moment.
lessons.topic: {{在|zài}} or {{正在|zhèngzài}} + a verb (+ {{呢|ne}}); {{没在|méi zài}}; {{…呢？|…ne?}} “where's…?”

dialog.r: Wéi, nǐ zài gàn shénme ne?
dialog.tr: Hi, what are you up to?

dialog.r: Wǒ zài zuò fàn ne. Nǐ ne?

blocks.p: **Going on now: {{在|zài}} + verb.** The same {{在|zài}} you know from places, before a verb, means “in the middle of”: {{我在做饭。|Wǒ zài zuò fàn.}} “I'm cooking.” {{正在|zhèngzài}} “right now” makes it stronger, and {{呢|ne}} at the end makes it sound natural and chatty: {{我正在吃饭呢。|Wǒ zhèngzài chīfàn ne.}}

table: He's in a meeting right now.

blocks.p: **What are you doing?** {{你在干什么？|Nǐ zài gàn shénme?}} or {{你在做什么？|Nǐ zài zuò shénme?}}: {{干|gàn}} “do” is the everyday spoken word. **Not doing it** is {{没在|méi zài}}: {{我没在睡觉。|Wǒ méi zài shuìjiào.}} “I'm not asleep.”

It works for the past too, with a time: {{昨天晚上八点我在看电视。|Zuótiān wǎnshang bā diǎn wǒ zài kàn diànshì.}} “At eight last night I was watching TV.” And **{{呢|ne}} after a noun** asks where it is: {{我的钥匙呢？|Wǒ de yàoshi ne?}} “Where are my keys?”

blocks.tip: To say where you're doing it, one {{在|zài}} is enough: {{我在家看书呢。|Wǒ zài jiā kàn shū ne.}} “I'm at home, reading.”

mistakes.why: {{在|zài}} goes before the verb: {{我在吃饭。|Wǒ zài chīfàn.}}
“Not in the middle of doing it” is {{没在|méi zài}}: {{我没在睡觉。|Wǒ méi zài shuìjiào.}}

lessons.title: Talk about things you've done before
lessons.summary: “Have you ever been to China?”, “I've seen it twice”, “I've never had Peking duck”: talk about your experiences with {{过|guo}}.
lessons.topic: Verb + {{过|guo}} “have ever done”; {{没…过|méi… guo}} “have never”; {{一次|yí cì}}, {{两次|liǎng cì}}

goal.tr: Have you ever been to China?

dialog.r: Nǐ qù guo Zhōngguó ma?
dialog.tr: Have you ever been to China?

dialog.t: 去过一次。我去过北京和上海。

dialog.tr: Once. I've been to Beijing and Shanghai.

blocks.p: **Ever: verb + {{过|guo}}.** {{过|guo}} after a verb says you've had the experience, at some time in your life: {{我去过中国。|Wǒ qù guo Zhōngguó.}} “I've been to China.” Ask with {{吗|ma}}: {{你吃过饺子吗？|Nǐ chī guo jiǎozi ma?}} “Have you ever had dumplings?” Answer with the verb and {{过|guo}}: {{吃过。|Chī guo.}}

**Never: {{没|méi}} + verb + {{过|guo}}.** Unlike {{了|le}}, {{过|guo}} stays after {{没|méi}}: {{我没去过中国。|Wǒ méi qù guo Zhōngguó.}} “I've never been to China.” Add {{从来|cónglái}} for “never ever”: {{我从来没吃过。|Wǒ cónglái méi chī guo.}}
**How many times?** {{次|cì}} “time” goes after the verb and {{过|guo}}: {{我去过两次。|Wǒ qù guo liǎng cì.}} “I've been twice.” {{几次？|Jǐ cì?}} is “How many times?”

table: you've done it at least once in your life
{{我去了北京。|Wǒ qù le Běijīng.}} I went to Beijing.
{{我去过北京。|Wǒ qù guo Běijīng.}} I've been to Beijing.
{{我没去北京。|Wǒ méi qù Běijīng.}} I didn't go.
{{我没去过北京。|Wǒ méi qù guo Běijīng.}} I've never been.

blocks.tip: {{过|guo}} is perfect for small talk: {{你吃过…吗？|Nǐ chī guo… ma?}}, {{你去过…吗？|Nǐ qù guo… ma?}} People love asking foreigners {{你吃过臭豆腐吗？|Nǐ chī guo chòudòufu ma?}} “Have you ever tried stinky tofu?”

lessons.title: Say how long
lessons.summary: “I've been learning Chinese for two years”, “I slept eight hours”, “How long did you wait?”: say how long things last.
lessons.topic: A length of time goes after the verb ({{学了两年|xué le liǎng nián}}); {{…了两年了|…le liǎng nián le}} (still going); {{多长时间|duō cháng shíjiān}}; {{从…到…|cóng… dào…}}

goal.r: Wǒ xué Zhōngwén xué le liǎng nián le.
goal.tr: I've been learning Chinese for two years.

dialog.t: 你的中文很好！你学了多长时间了？
dialog.r: Nǐ de Zhōngwén hěn hǎo! Nǐ xué le duō cháng shíjiān le?
dialog.tr: Your Chinese is very good! How long have you been learning?

dialog.t: 哪里哪里！我学了两年了。
dialog.r: Nǎlǐ nǎlǐ! Wǒ xué le liǎng nián le.
dialog.tr: Oh, not really! I've been learning for two years.

dialog.r: Nǐ měitiān xué jǐ ge xiǎoshí?

dialog.t: 一个小时。我从八点学到九点。
dialog.r: Yí ge xiǎoshí. Wǒ cóng bā diǎn xué dào jiǔ diǎn.
dialog.tr: One hour. I study from eight to nine.

blocks.p: **How long goes after the verb.** A length of time comes after the verb: the opposite of a point in time, which goes before it. {{我睡了八个小时。|Wǒ shuì le bā ge xiǎoshí.}} “I slept for eight hours.” {{我等了二十分钟。|Wǒ děng le èrshí fēnzhōng.}} “I waited twenty minutes.”

table: A point in time: before the verb
A length of time: after the verb
{{我八点睡觉。|Wǒ bā diǎn shuìjiào.}} I go to bed at eight.
{{我睡了八个小时。|Wǒ shuì le bā ge xiǎoshí.}} I slept for eight hours.
{{我明天学习。|Wǒ míngtiān xuéxí.}} I'll study tomorrow.
{{我学习了两个小时。|Wǒ xuéxí le liǎng ge xiǎoshí.}} I studied for two hours.

blocks.p: **With an object, say the verb twice**, or put the time before the object: {{我学中文学了两年。|Wǒ xué Zhōngwén xué le liǎng nián.}} = {{我学了两年中文。|Wǒ xué le liǎng nián Zhōngwén.}} “I studied Chinese for two years.”

**Still going: a second {{了|le}} at the end.** {{我学了两年。|Wǒ xué le liǎng nián.}} “I studied for two years” (maybe I've stopped). {{我学了两年了。|Wǒ xué le liǎng nián le.}} “I've been studying for two years” (and I still am): it's the {{了|le}} of something new. **How long?** {{多长时间？|Duō cháng shíjiān?}} or {{多久？|Duō jiǔ?}}

blocks.tip: Lengths of time: {{五分钟|wǔ fēnzhōng}} five minutes, {{两个小时|liǎng ge xiǎoshí}} two hours, {{三天|sān tiān}} three days, {{一个星期|yí ge xīngqī}} a week, {{六个月|liù ge yuè}} six months, {{两年|liǎng nián}} two years. Hours, weeks and months take {{个|ge}}; minutes, days and years don't.

lessons.title: Compare two things
lessons.summary: “Today is colder than yesterday”, “This one's a bit cheaper”, “I'm not as tall as my brother”: compare people and things.
lessons.topic: A {{比|bǐ}} B + adjective (no {{很|hěn}}); {{一点儿|yìdiǎnr}}, {{多了|duō le}}; A {{没有|méiyǒu}} B ({{那么|nàme}}) + adjective

dialog.r: Zhège shǒujī bǐ nàge guì ma?
dialog.tr: Is this phone more expensive than that one?

dialog.t: 贵一点儿。这个比那个好多了。

blocks.p: **A {{比|bǐ}} B + adjective.** {{比|bǐ}} means “compared with”: {{今天比昨天冷。|Jīntiān bǐ zuótiān lěng.}} “Today is colder than yesterday” (“today compared-with yesterday cold”). The adjective never changes (no “-er”, no “more”), and there's **no {{很|hěn}}** in a comparison.

**How much more?** Say it after the adjective: {{一点儿|yìdiǎnr}} “a bit”, {{多了|duō le}} “much”: {{这个比那个贵一点儿。|Zhège bǐ nàge guì yìdiǎnr.}} “This one is a bit more expensive.” {{他比我高多了。|Tā bǐ wǒ gāo duō le.}} “He's much taller than me.” Or {{更|gèng}} “even more” before the adjective: {{明天更冷。|Míngtiān gèng lěng.}} “Tomorrow will be even colder.”

**Not as… as**: A {{没有|méiyǒu}} B ({{那么|nàme}}) + adjective: {{我没有我哥哥那么高。|Wǒ méiyǒu wǒ gēge nàme gāo.}} “I'm not as tall as my brother.” ({{不比|bù bǐ}} exists too, but it means “no more … than”, which is rarely what you want.)

table: {{这个比那个便宜一点儿。|Zhège bǐ nàge piányi yìdiǎnr.}}
This one's a bit cheaper than that one.
{{他比我高多了。|Tā bǐ wǒ gāo duō le.}}
{{我没有他那么忙。|Wǒ méiyǒu tā nàme máng.}}

blocks.tip: {{大|dà}} “big” also means “older” for people, and {{小|xiǎo}} “younger”: {{我妹妹比我小三岁。|Wǒ mèimei bǐ wǒ xiǎo sān suì.}} “My sister is three years younger than me.”

blocks.p: **The same: A {{跟|gēn}} B {{一样|yíyàng}}.** {{跟|gēn}} (or {{和|hé}}) “with”, then {{一样|yíyàng}} “the same”: {{你的手机跟我的一样。|Nǐ de shǒujī gēn wǒ de yíyàng.}} “Your phone is the same as mine.” Add an adjective for “as … as”: {{我跟他一样高。|Wǒ gēn tā yíyàng gāo.}} “I'm as tall as him.”
**Different** is {{不一样|bù yíyàng}}: {{中国菜跟美国菜很不一样。|Zhōngguó cài gēn Měiguó cài hěn bù yíyàng.}} “Chinese food is very different from American food.”

**The most: {{最|zuì}} + adjective.** {{最|zuì}} goes before the adjective, like {{很|hěn}}: {{这个最好。|Zhège zuì hǎo.}} “This one is the best.” Before a noun, add {{的|de}}: {{最贵的菜|zuì guì de cài}} “the most expensive dish”, {{最好的朋友|zuì hǎo de péngyou}} “best friend”. Where it's the most comes first: {{班里最高的|bān li zuì gāo de}} “the tallest in the class”.

lessons.title: Say how well someone does something
lessons.summary: “You speak Chinese really well!”, “He runs fast”, “How did you sleep?”: describe how something is done, with {{得|de}}.
lessons.topic: Verb + {{得|de}} + how: {{说得很好|shuō de hěn hǎo}}; with an object: {{(说)中文说得很好|(shuō) Zhōngwén shuō de hěn hǎo}}; {{…得怎么样？|…de zěnmeyàng?}}

goal.r: Nǐ Zhōngwén shuō de hěn hǎo!

dialog.r: Nǐ zuò fàn zuò de zhēn hǎo!
dialog.tr: You're a really good cook!

dialog.r: Xièxie! Cài zuò de zěnmeyàng?
dialog.tr: Thanks! How was the food?

dialog.r: Fēicháng hǎochī! Nǐ Zhōngwén yě shuō de hěn hǎo.

blocks.p: **How it's done: verb + {{得|de}} + description.** English says “runs fast”; Chinese says “runs-*de* fast”, with the description after {{得|de}}: {{他跑得很快。|Tā pǎo de hěn kuài.}} “He runs fast.” {{我昨天睡得不好。|Wǒ zuótiān shuì de bù hǎo.}} “I didn't sleep well last night.” The description is an adjective, usually with {{很|hěn}}, {{太…了|tài… le}} or {{不|bù}}.

blocks.means: a word or phrase after a verb that completes it: how well the action was done, or what came of it. “Well” in “speaks well”.

blocks.p: **With an object, say the verb twice**, as with “how long”: {{她说中文说得很好。|Tā shuō Zhōngwén shuō de hěn hǎo.}} Or put the object first and say the verb once: {{她中文说得很好。|Tā Zhōngwén shuō de hěn hǎo.}} Either way, a verb comes right before {{得|de}}.
**How did it go?** {{…得怎么样？|…de zěnmeyàng?}}: {{你考得怎么样？|Nǐ kǎo de zěnmeyàng?}} “How did your exam go?” {{你睡得怎么样？|Nǐ shuì de zěnmeyàng?}} “How did you sleep?”

lessons.title: Say a bit, too, and not at all
lessons.summary: “It's a bit expensive”, “A bit slower, please”, “It's not hard at all”: soften what you say, or make it stronger.
lessons.topic: {{有点儿|yǒudiǎnr}} + adjective (a bit too) vs adjective + {{一点儿|yìdiǎnr}} (a bit more); {{太…了|tài… le}}; {{不太|bú tài}}; {{一点儿也不|yìdiǎnr yě bù}}

goal.tr: This top is a bit expensive.

dialog.r: Cài zěnmeyàng?
dialog.tr: How's the food?

dialog.r: Hěn hǎochī, jiùshì yǒudiǎnr là.
dialog.tr: Delicious, just a bit spicy.

dialog.tr: Would you like some water?

dialog.t: 好，谢谢！我朋友一点儿也不怕辣。

blocks.p: **A bit (too): {{有点儿|yǒudiǎnr}} + adjective.** Before an adjective, {{有点儿|yǒudiǎnr}} means “a bit, rather”, and it's for things you're not happy about: {{有点儿贵|yǒudiǎnr guì}} “a bit expensive”, {{有点儿累|yǒudiǎnr lèi}} “a bit tired”.

**A bit more: adjective + {{一点儿|yìdiǎnr}}.** After an adjective, {{一点儿|yìdiǎnr}} compares: “a bit more …”. It's how you ask for something different: {{便宜一点儿吧！|Piányi yìdiǎnr ba!}} “A bit cheaper!” {{请说慢一点儿。|Qǐng shuō màn yìdiǎnr.}} “A bit more slowly, please.” Before a noun, {{一点儿|yìdiǎnr}} is “some, a little”: {{喝一点儿水|hē yìdiǎnr shuǐ}} “drink some water”.

table: {{这件大一点儿。|Zhè jiàn dà yìdiǎnr.}}
{{一点儿也不冷。|Yìdiǎnr yě bù lěng.}}

blocks.p: **Stronger or softer.** {{太…了|tài… le}} “too, so”; {{不太|bú tài}} “not very”, a gentle “no”; {{一点儿也不|yìdiǎnr yě bù}} “not at all”: {{中文一点儿也不难！|Zhōngwén yìdiǎnr yě bù nán!}} “Chinese isn't hard at all!”

ex.tr: This top is a bit expensive.
Do you have anything a bit cheaper?

blocks.tip: In quick speech {{一点儿|yìdiǎnr}} often drops its {{一|yì}}: {{喝点儿水|hē diǎnr shuǐ}} “have some water”. In the south you'll hear {{一点|yìdiǎn}} and {{有点|yǒudiǎn}}, without the {{儿|r}}.

mistakes.tr: Could you speak a bit more slowly?
mistakes.why: Asking for “a bit more”: the adjective, then {{一点儿|yìdiǎnr}}. {{有点儿|yǒudiǎnr}} is for complaints.
Before an adjective, “a bit” is {{有点儿|yǒudiǎnr}}: {{今天有点儿冷。|Jīntiān yǒudiǎnr lěng.}}

lessons.title: Say which one you mean
lessons.summary: “The book I bought yesterday”, “the woman in red”, “What you said is right”: describe a person or thing with a whole phrase.
lessons.topic: A describing phrase + {{的|de}} + the noun, always before it: {{我昨天买的书|wǒ zuótiān mǎi de shū}}, {{穿红衣服的人|chuān hóng yīfu de rén}}

goal.r: Zhè shì wǒ zuótiān mǎi de shū.
goal.tr: This is the book I bought yesterday.

dialog.r: Nàge chuān hóng yīfu de rén shì shéi?
dialog.tr: Who's that woman in red?

dialog.tr: Which one?

dialog.tr: The one on the phone by the door.

blocks.p: **Everything that describes a noun goes before it, joined by {{的|de}}.** English puts a long description after the noun: “the book *that I bought yesterday*”. Chinese puts it before, and joins it with {{的|de}}, just as it does with owners: {{我昨天买的书|wǒ zuótiān mǎi de shū}}, word for word “I yesterday bought -*de* book”.

**No “who”, “which” or “that”**: {{的|de}} does all their work. Once the noun is known, it can be left out: {{你说的对。|Nǐ shuō de duì.}} “What you said is right.” {{我要红的。|Wǒ yào hóng de.}} “I'd like the red one.”
**With “this” or “that”**, the description usually comes first: {{我昨天买的那本书|wǒ zuótiān mǎi de nà běn shū}} “that book I bought yesterday”.

ex.r: Zhè shì wǒ zuótiān mǎi de shū.
ex.tr: This is the book I bought yesterday.

ex.tr: The film we saw yesterday was really interesting.

ex.r: Zài Zhōngguó gōngzuò de wàiguórén hěn duō.

blocks.tip: After a short adjective, {{的|de}} is often dropped: {{好朋友|hǎo péngyou}} “good friend”, {{新手机|xīn shǒujī}} “new phone”. In speech, keep descriptions short: say {{那个人|nàge rén}} first, then add the detail.

lessons.title: Say whether you got it done
lessons.summary: “I've finished”, “I didn't understand”, “I found it!”, “I wrote it wrong”: say what came of an action.
lessons.topic: Verb + result: {{完|wán}}, {{懂|dǒng}}, {{到|dào}}, {{见|jiàn}}, {{好|hǎo}}, {{错|cuò}}; {{没|méi}} + verb + result

dialog.r: Bàogào xiěwán le ma?
dialog.tr: Have you finished the report?

dialog.r: Xiěwán le, wǒ fā gěi nǐ le.
dialog.tr: Yes, I've sent it to you.

dialog.r: Wǒ méi kàndào.
dialog.tr: I haven't seen it.

dialog.t: 是吗？对不起，我写错邮箱了！
dialog.r: Shì ma? Duìbuqǐ, wǒ xiěcuò yóuxiāng le!

dialog.r: Méi guānxi. Xiànzài shōudào le!

blocks.p: **What came of it: verb + result.** A Chinese verb often says only the attempt: {{听|tīng}} “listen”, {{看|kàn}} “look”, {{找|zhǎo}} “look for”. A second word right after it says the result: {{听懂|tīngdǒng}} “listen-understand”, {{看见|kànjiàn}} “look-see”, {{找到|zhǎodào}} “look for-reach”, that is, find. The two act as one verb, with {{了|le}} after both: {{我找到了！|Wǒ zhǎodào le!}} “I've found it!”

table: {{吃完|chīwán}} finish eating, {{做完|zuòwán}} finish doing
{{找到|zhǎodào}} find, {{买到|mǎidào}} manage to buy, {{收到|shōudào}} receive
{{做好|zuòhǎo}} get ready, {{准备好|zhǔnbèi hǎo}} be prepared

blocks.p: **It didn't work out: {{没|méi}} + verb + result**, with no {{了|le}}: {{我没听懂。|Wǒ méi tīngdǒng.}} “I didn't understand” (I listened, but didn't get it). {{我没找到。|Wǒ méi zhǎodào.}} “I didn't find it.” The result matters: {{我没听|wǒ méi tīng}} “I didn't listen” is quite another excuse!

blocks.p: **Can or can't manage: {{得|de}} or {{不|bu}} between the verb and its result.** Put {{得|de}} inside a verb + result for “can”, and {{不|bu}} for “can't”: {{听懂|tīngdǒng}} “understand” becomes {{听得懂|tīng de dǒng}} “can understand” and {{听不懂|tīng bu dǒng}} “can't understand”. Both little words are said lightly, as part of one word.

**Why not just {{不能|bù néng}}?** {{不能|bù néng}} is about not being allowed, or something outside stopping you. The {{不|bu}} form says the result can't be reached, however hard you try: {{我听不懂|wǒ tīng bu dǒng}} “I can't understand (it's beyond me)”. And {{来不了|lái bu liǎo}} is the everyday way to say you can't make it.
**Asking**: {{你听得懂吗？|Nǐ tīng de dǒng ma?}} or, A-not-A, {{你听得懂听不懂？|Nǐ tīng de dǒng tīng bu dǒng?}} “Can you understand?”

lessons.title: Ask the way and give directions
lessons.summary: “How do I get to the station?”, “Go straight on, then turn left”, “Come in!”, “He's gone out”: directions and movement.
lessons.topic: {{怎么走？|zěnme zǒu?}}; {{往|wǎng}} + direction + verb; {{来|lai}} and {{去|qu}} after a verb: {{进来|jìnlai}}, {{出去|chūqu}}, {{回来|huílai}}

goal.tr: Excuse me, how do I get to the railway station?

blocks.p: **Asking the way**: the place + {{怎么走？|zěnme zǒu?}}, “how (do I) walk?”: {{地铁站怎么走？|Dìtiězhàn zěnme zǒu?}} Or {{…在哪儿？|…zài nǎr?}}, which you already know.

**Giving directions**: {{往|wǎng}} “towards” + a direction + the verb: {{往前走|wǎng qián zǒu}} “go straight ahead”, {{往左拐|wǎng zuǒ guǎi}} “turn left”. {{一直|yìzhí}} is “all the way, straight on”. {{到|dào}} + a place: “when you get to…”.

**Coming and going: {{来|lai}} and {{去|qu}} after a verb.** After a verb of movement, {{来|lai}} means towards the speaker and {{去|qu}} away from the speaker: {{进来|jìnlai}} “come in”, {{进去|jìnqu}} “go in”, {{出去|chūqu}} “go out”, {{回来|huílai}} “come back”, {{上去|shàngqu}} “go up”, {{下来|xiàlai}} “come down”. A place goes in the middle: {{上楼去|shàng lóu qu}} “go upstairs”, {{进教室来|jìn jiàoshì lai}} “come into the classroom”.

lessons.title: Give advice and say what's needed
lessons.summary: “You should rest”, “I have to go”, “You don't need to come”, “Don't worry!”: give advice, say what's needed, and tell people not to.
lessons.topic: {{应该|yīnggāi}} “should”; {{得|děi}} and {{要|yào}} “have to”; {{不用|búyòng}} “don't need to”; {{别|bié}} / {{不要|búyào}} “don't!”

dialog.r: Wǒ tóu téng, yǒudiǎnr fāshāo.

blocks.p: **Should: {{应该|yīnggāi}}** + verb, for advice and what's right: {{你应该去看医生。|Nǐ yīnggāi qù kàn yīshēng.}} “You should see a doctor.” Shouldn't: {{不应该|bù yīnggāi}}.

**Have to: {{得|děi}} or {{要|yào}}.** In speech, {{得|děi}} (the character you know as {{得|de}}, here said děi) means “have to”: {{我得走了。|Wǒ děi zǒu le.}} “I have to go now.” {{要|yào}}, which you know as “want” and “will”, also means “need to”: {{你要多喝水。|Nǐ yào duō hē shuǐ.}} “You need to drink lots of water.”
**Don't need to: {{不用|búyòng}}.** “Not have to” is never {{不得|bù děi}}; it's {{不用|búyòng}}: {{你不用来。|Nǐ búyòng lái.}} “You don't need to come.” {{不用谢！|Búyòng xiè!}} “No need to thank me!”

**Don't!: {{别|bié}} or {{不要|búyào}}** + verb: {{别担心！|Bié dānxīn!}} “Don't worry!” {{不要在这儿抽烟。|Búyào zài zhèr chōuyān.}} “Don't smoke here.” {{别|bié}} is friendly and spoken; {{不要|búyào}} is firmer, and the one on signs.

lessons.topic: {{要…了|yào… le}}, {{快…了|kuài… le}}, {{快要…了|kuàiyào… le}}, {{就要…了|jiùyào… le}}

dialog.r: Kuài diǎnr! Huǒchē kuàiyào kāi le!

blocks.p: **About to: {{要…了|yào… le}}.** Put {{要|yào}} before the verb and {{了|le}} at the end: {{下雨了|xiàyǔ le}} is “it's started raining”, and {{要下雨了|yào xiàyǔ le}} is “it's going to rain any minute”. {{快要|kuàiyào}} (or just {{快|kuài}}) “soon” brings it even closer: {{火车快要开了。|Huǒchē kuàiyào kāi le.}} “The train's about to leave.”
**With a time, use {{就要…了|jiùyào… le}}.** {{快|kuài}} can't go with a time word, but {{就要|jiùyào}} can: {{我下个星期就要去北京了。|Wǒ xià ge xīngqī jiùyào qù Běijīng le.}} “I'm off to Beijing next week.”
**Nearly, with a number or a noun**: {{快…了|kuài… le}}: {{快十二点了。|Kuài shí'èr diǎn le.}} “It's nearly twelve.” {{快春节了！|Kuài Chūnjié le!}} “It's nearly Spring Festival!”

lessons.summary: “Why are you learning Chinese?”, “Because I want to work in China”, “It rained, so we stayed in”: ask for reasons and give them.
lessons.topic: {{为什么|wèishénme}}; {{因为…所以…|yīnwèi… suǒyǐ…}}: Chinese likes both halves

blocks.p: **Why?** {{为什么|wèishénme}} goes before the verb, where a reason would go: {{你为什么学中文？|Nǐ wèishénme xué Zhōngwén?}} “Why are you learning Chinese?” {{你为什么没来？|Nǐ wèishénme méi lái?}} “Why didn't you come?” Like every question word, it takes no {{吗|ma}}.

**Because… so…** English uses one or the other; Chinese happily uses both. {{因为|yīnwèi}} “because” starts the reason and {{所以|suǒyǐ}} “so” starts the result: {{因为下雨了，所以我们没出去。|Yīnwèi xiàyǔ le, suǒyǐ wǒmen méi chūqù.}} “It was raining, so we didn't go out.” Either half can also stand alone.
**The reason usually comes first.** In an answer to {{为什么|wèishénme}}, {{因为…|yīnwèi…}} alone is enough: {{因为我很忙。|Yīnwèi wǒ hěn máng.}} “Because I'm busy.”

blocks.p: **But**: {{但是|dànshì}}, {{可是|kěshì}} or {{不过|búguò}}, at the start of the second part. They mean the same; {{可是|kěshì}} is very spoken, and {{不过|búguò}} softer, like “though”.

**Although… but…** English never says “although… but”; Chinese nearly always does: {{虽然|suīrán}} “although” starts the first part, and {{但是|dànshì}} or {{可是|kěshì}} starts the second: {{虽然我很累，但是很开心。|Suīrán wǒ hěn lèi, dànshì hěn kāixīn.}} “Although I'm tired, I'm happy.” {{虽然|suīrán}} can also come after the subject: {{我虽然很累，…|Wǒ suīrán hěn lèi, …}}

**Still**: {{还是|háishi}}, before the verb in the second part: {{虽然下雨了，我们还是去了。|Suīrán xiàyǔ le, wǒmen háishi qù le.}} “It was raining, but we still went.” It's the {{还是|háishi}} of “or” questions, doing another job.

goal.t: 如果明天下雨，我们就不去了。

blocks.p: **If: {{如果|rúguǒ}}**, or the more spoken {{要是|yàoshi}}, starts the condition, and {{就|jiù}} “then” comes in the second part: {{如果明天下雨，我们就不去了。|Rúguǒ míngtiān xiàyǔ, wǒmen jiù bú qù le.}} {{的话|dehuà}} at the end of the first part is common in speech: {{要是下雨的话|yàoshi xiàyǔ dehuà}} “if it rains”.

**{{就|jiù}} goes after the subject**, just before the verb (or before {{不|bù}}, {{会|huì}}, {{要|yào}}): {{如果你有时间，我们就去。|Rúguǒ nǐ yǒu shíjiān, wǒmen jiù qù.}} Never before the subject. The condition comes first, and there's still no future tense: the situation says it.

table: {{就休息一下吧。|jiù xiūxi yíxià ba.}}
If you're tired, take a break.
{{要是太贵的话，|Yàoshi tài guì dehuà,}}
{{我就不买了。|wǒ jiù bù mǎi le.}}
If it's too expensive, I won't buy it.
{{就来我家吧。|jiù lái wǒ jiā ba.}}
If you have time, come round.

blocks.p: In a short, chatty sentence {{如果|rúguǒ}} can be dropped, and {{就|jiù}} alone does the job: {{你有时间就来吧。|Nǐ yǒu shíjiān jiù lái ba.}} “Come if you have time.”

dialog.t: 不，我小的时候只喜欢玩儿游戏！
dialog.r: Bù, wǒ xiǎo de shíhou zhǐ xǐhuan wánr yóuxì!
dialog.tr: No, when I was little I only liked playing games!

blocks.p: **Before, after, when: at the end of the event.** English says “*after* work”; Chinese says “work *after*”: {{下班以后|xiàbān yǐhòu}}. The same goes for {{以前|yǐqián}} “before” and {{的时候|de shíhou}} “when, while”: {{吃饭以前|chīfàn yǐqián}} “before eating”, {{我在中国的时候|wǒ zài Zhōngguó de shíhou}} “when I was in China”. The whole time phrase comes first, like any time word.

**First…, then…** {{先|xiān}}… {{再|zài}}… is “first this, then that”, for plans and instructions: {{你先洗手，再吃饭。|Nǐ xiān xǐ shǒu, zài chīfàn.}} “Wash your hands first, then eat.” ({{然后|ránhòu}} works too.)
**As soon as: {{一…就…|yī… jiù…}}.** {{一|yī}} before the first verb, {{就|jiù}} before the second: {{我一到家就给你打电话。|Wǒ yí dào jiā jiù gěi nǐ dǎ diànhuà.}} “I'll call you as soon as I get home.”

ex.tr: After work, I go to the gym.
Don't look at your phone before bed.

ex.t: 我在北京的时候，常常吃烤鸭。
ex.r: Wǒ zài Běijīng de shíhou, chángcháng chī kǎoyā.
ex.tr: When I was in Beijing, I often ate roast duck.

ex.r: Nǐ xiān xǐ shǒu, zài chīfàn.
ex.tr: Wash your hands first, then eat.

ex.t: 我一到家就给你打电话。
ex.r: Wǒ yí dào jiā jiù gěi nǐ dǎ diànhuà.
ex.tr: I'll call you as soon as I get home.

ex.r: Tā yì hē jiǔ jiù liǎn hóng.
ex.tr: As soon as he drinks, his face goes red.

blocks.tip: {{以前|yǐqián}} on its own means “before, in the past”: {{我以前不喜欢吃辣的。|Wǒ yǐqián bù xǐhuan chī là de.}} “I didn't use to like spicy food.” And {{以后|yǐhòu}} alone means “later, in future”: {{以后再说吧。|Yǐhòu zài shuō ba.}} “Let's talk about it later.”

mistakes.tr: After work, I go to the gym.
mistakes.why: {{以后|yǐhòu}} goes after the event: {{下班以后|xiàbān yǐhòu}} “work after”.

mistakes.why: {{一|yī}} before the first verb, {{就|jiù}} before the second: {{一到家就打电话|yí dào jiā jiù dǎ diànhuà}}.

lessons.title: Give your opinion and your reasons
lessons.summary: “I think the train is better”, “For me, the price matters most”, “I agree”, “Not necessarily”: say what you think, and why.
lessons.topic: {{我觉得|wǒ juéde}}, {{我认为|wǒ rènwéi}}; {{对…来说|duì… lái shuō}}; {{同意|tóngyì}}; {{不一定|bù yídìng}}; {{而且|érqiě}}

goal.t: 我觉得坐高铁比坐飞机方便。
goal.r: Wǒ juéde zuò gāotiě bǐ zuò fēijī fāngbiàn.
goal.tr: I think the high-speed train is more convenient than flying.

dialog.t: 去上海，你觉得坐飞机好还是坐高铁好？
dialog.r: Qù Shànghǎi, nǐ juéde zuò fēijī hǎo háishi zuò gāotiě hǎo?
dialog.tr: To get to Shanghai, do you think flying or the high-speed train is better?

dialog.t: 我觉得坐高铁好，因为不用很早去机场。
dialog.r: Wǒ juéde zuò gāotiě hǎo, yīnwèi búyòng hěn zǎo qù jīchǎng.
dialog.tr: I think the train is better, because you don't have to get to the airport early.

dialog.t: 我同意。而且坐高铁也很舒服。
dialog.r: Wǒ tóngyì. Érqiě zuò gāotiě yě hěn shūfu.
dialog.tr: I agree. And the train's comfortable too.

dialog.t: 对我来说，最重要的是便宜！
dialog.r: Duì wǒ lái shuō, zuì zhòngyào de shì piányi!
dialog.tr: For me, the most important thing is the price!

dialog.t: 那不一定，有时候飞机票更便宜。
dialog.r: Nà bù yídìng, yǒu shíhou fēijīpiào gèng piányi.
dialog.tr: Not necessarily: sometimes plane tickets are cheaper.

blocks.p: **I think: {{我觉得|wǒ juéde}}** + your opinion, as a whole sentence: {{我觉得中文很有意思。|Wǒ juéde Zhōngwén hěn yǒu yìsi.}} {{我认为|wǒ rènwéi}} is more formal, for serious opinions. Ask with {{你觉得…？|Nǐ juéde…?}}, or simply {{你觉得呢？|Nǐ juéde ne?}} “What do you think?”
**For me, as far as … is concerned: {{对…来说|duì… lái shuō}}**, at the start: {{对我来说，太贵了。|Duì wǒ lái shuō, tài guì le.}} “For me, it's too expensive.” {{对学生来说|duì xuésheng lái shuō}} “for students”.

**Agreeing and disagreeing**: {{我同意。|Wǒ tóngyì.}} “I agree.” {{我不同意。|Wǒ bù tóngyì.}} “I disagree.” Softer, and more Chinese: {{不一定。|Bù yídìng.}} “Not necessarily.” **To add another reason**, {{而且|érqiě}} “and what's more”, as well as the {{因为|yīnwèi}} you know.

table: {{我觉得这个主意不错。|Wǒ juéde zhège zhǔyi búcuò.}}
I think it's a good idea.
{{对我来说，健康最重要。|Duì wǒ lái shuō, jiànkāng zuì zhòngyào.}}
{{我同意你的看法。|Wǒ tóngyì nǐ de kànfǎ.}}

ex.t: 我觉得坐高铁比坐飞机方便。
ex.r: Wǒ juéde zuò gāotiě bǐ zuò fēijī fāngbiàn.
ex.tr: I think the high-speed train is more convenient than flying.

ex.t: 你觉得这部电影怎么样？
ex.r: Nǐ juéde zhè bù diànyǐng zěnmeyàng?
ex.tr: What did you think of the film?

ex.t: 我觉得有点儿贵，不过质量很好。
ex.r: Wǒ juéde yǒudiǎnr guì, búguò zhìliàng hěn hǎo.
ex.tr: I think it's a bit pricey, but the quality is good.

ex.t: 对孩子来说，玩儿也很重要。
ex.r: Duì háizi lái shuō, wánr yě hěn zhòngyào.

ex.t: 我不同意。我觉得在家工作更好。
ex.r: Wǒ bù tóngyì. Wǒ juéde zài jiā gōngzuò gèng hǎo.
ex.tr: I disagree. I think working from home is better.

blocks.tip: Chinese conversation tends to avoid a flat “No, you're wrong.” {{不一定|bù yídìng}} “not necessarily”, {{也有道理|yě yǒu dàoli}} “that's a fair point too” and {{我觉得…|wǒ juéde…}} keep things friendly.

mistakes.tr: I think Chinese is really interesting.
mistakes.why: After {{我觉得|wǒ juéde}} comes an ordinary sentence, and an adjective still takes no {{是|shì}}.

lessons.title: Say when, where and how it happened
lessons.summary: “When did you get here?” “Last night, by train.” Ask and tell the details of something that has already happened.
lessons.topic: {{是…的|shì… de}} around the detail of a past event: when, where, how, with whom; {{不是…的|bú shì… de}}

goal.r: Wǒ shì zuò huǒchē lái de.

dialog.t: 欢迎！你是什么时候到的？
dialog.r: Huānyíng! Nǐ shì shénme shíhou dào de?
dialog.tr: Welcome! When did you get here?

dialog.r: Wǒ shì zuótiān wǎnshang dào de.
dialog.tr: I got here last night.

dialog.r: Nǐ shì zuò fēijī lái de ma?
dialog.tr: Did you fly?

dialog.r: Bú shì, wǒ shì zuò gāotiě lái de.
dialog.tr: No, I came on the high-speed train.

dialog.r: Gēn shéi yìqǐ lái de?
dialog.tr: Who did you come with?

dialog.r: Wǒ shì yí ge rén lái de.
dialog.tr: I came on my own.

blocks.p: **The event is known; the detail is the news.** When everyone knows something happened, and you want to ask or tell *when*, *where*, *how* or *with whom*, put {{是|shì}} before that detail and {{的|de}} at the end: {{我是昨天到的。|Wǒ shì zuótiān dào de.}} “It was yesterday that I arrived.” The spotlight falls on what comes right after {{是|shì}}.

table: {{我是去年来的。|Wǒ shì qùnián lái de.}}
{{这件衣服是在北京买的。|Zhè jiàn yīfu shì zài Běijīng mǎi de.}}
I bought this top in Beijing.
{{我们是打车去的。|Wǒmen shì dǎchē qù de.}}
{{他是跟朋友一起去的。|Tā shì gēn péngyou yìqǐ qù de.}}
{{这是我妈妈做的。|Zhè shì wǒ māma zuò de.}}

blocks.p: **{{了|le}} or {{是…的|shì… de}}?** {{了|le}} tells that something happened: {{他来了。|Tā lái le.}} “He's come.” Once that's known, the questions about it take {{是…的|shì… de}}: {{他是怎么来的？|Tā shì zěnme lái de?}} “How did he get here?” In speech {{是|shì}} is often dropped, but never the {{的|de}}: {{你什么时候到的？|Nǐ shénme shíhou dào de?}}
**Not**: {{不是…的|bú shì… de}}: {{我不是坐飞机来的。|Wǒ bú shì zuò fēijī lái de.}} “I didn't come by plane.”

ex.r: Wǒ shì zuò huǒchē lái de.
Nǐ shì shénme shíhou dào de?
Nǐ shì zài nǎr xué de Zhōngwén?
ex.note: with an object, {{的|de}} often goes before it

ex.r: Wǒmen shì zài dàxué rènshi de.

ex.t: 这个蛋糕是我自己做的。
ex.r: Zhège dàngāo shì wǒ zìjǐ zuò de.
Wǒ bú shì yí ge rén lái de.

blocks.tip: This pattern is perfect for small talk with new people: {{你是哪年来中国的？|Nǐ shì nǎ nián lái Zhōngguó de?}} “What year did you come to China?”, {{你们是怎么认识的？|Nǐmen shì zěnme rènshi de?}} “How did you two meet?”

mistakes.why: With {{是…的|shì… de}} there's no {{了|le}}: {{我是昨天到的。|Wǒ shì zuótiān dào de.}}
Don't forget the {{的|de}} at the end: it closes the detail.

practice.q: Choose the missing word.

lessons.title: Say what you did with something
lessons.summary: “Put your phone on the table”, “I've finished my homework”, “Don't forget your keys!”: say what you do to a particular thing.
lessons.topic: {{把|bǎ}} + the thing + verb + what happens to it: {{把门关上|bǎ mén guānshang}}, {{把手机放在桌子上|bǎ shǒujī fàng zài zhuōzi shang}}

goal.r: Qǐng bǎ shǒujī fàng zài zhuōzi shang.
goal.tr: Please put your phone on the table.

dialog.r: Nǐ bǎ hùzhào fàng zài nǎr le?
dialog.tr: Where did you put your passport?

dialog.r: Wǒ bǎ tā fàng zài bāo li le.
dialog.tr: I put it in my bag.

dialog.t: 好。别把手机充电器忘了！
dialog.r: Hǎo. Bié bǎ shǒujī chōngdiànqì wàng le!
dialog.tr: Good. Don't forget your phone charger!

dialog.t: 已经带了。妈，你能把窗户关上吗？有点儿冷。
dialog.r: Yǐjīng dài le. Mā, nǐ néng bǎ chuānghu guānshang ma? Yǒudiǎnr lěng.
dialog.tr: Already packed. Mum, can you close the window? It's a bit cold.

blocks.p: **{{把|bǎ}}: take the thing, and do something to it.** {{把|bǎ}} brings a particular, known thing before the verb, to say what happens to it: {{我把门关上了。|Wǒ bǎ mén guānshang le.}} “I closed the door” (“I took the door and closed it”). The order: who + {{把|bǎ}} + the thing + verb + the result, or where it ends up.

table: Please put your phone on the table.

blocks.p: **The verb can't stand alone.** After {{把|bǎ}} the verb needs something more: a result ({{做完|zuòwán}}), a place ({{放在包里|fàng zài bāo li}}), a direction ({{拿出来|ná chūlai}} “take out”) or {{了|le}}. {{我把门关。|Wǒ bǎ mén guān.}} on its own sounds unfinished. And the thing is a particular one, “the door”, “my phone”, never “a door”.

**When is it needed?** Mostly for moving, putting, giving and changing things, and in instructions: {{把…放在|bǎ… fàng zài}} “put … in, on”, {{把…给我|bǎ… gěi wǒ}} “give me …”, {{把…带来|bǎ… dàilai}} “bring …”. {{不|bù}}, {{没|méi}} and {{别|bié}} go before {{把|bǎ}}: {{别把手机忘了！|Bié bǎ shǒujī wàng le!}}

ex.r: Qǐng bǎ shǒujī fàng zài zhuōzi shang.
ex.tr: Please put your phone on the table.

ex.r: Nǐ bǎ hùzhào fàng zài nǎr le?
ex.tr: Where did you put your passport?

ex.r: Tā hái méi bǎ qián huán gěi wǒ.
ex.tr: He still hasn't paid me back.
ex.note: {{还|hái}} “still”, and {{还|huán}} “give back”: one character, two words

blocks.tip: {{放在|fàng zài}} “put in”, {{住在|zhù zài}} “live in”, {{坐在|zuò zài}} “sit in”: with verbs of putting, living and sitting, {{在|zài}} + place comes after the verb, to say where something ends up.

mistakes.why: After {{把|bǎ}} the verb needs something more: a result, a place, or {{了|le}}. {{我把门关上了。|Wǒ bǎ mén guānshang le.}}

mistakes.tr: I put the phone on the table.
mistakes.why: Where a thing ends up goes after the verb, so the thing itself moves before it, with {{把|bǎ}}: {{我把手机放在桌子上。|Wǒ bǎ shǒujī fàng zài zhuōzi shang.}}

practice.q: Choose the missing word.
practice.why: The thing comes before the verb with {{把|bǎ}}.

options: {{我把钥匙放在包里了。|Wǒ bǎ yàoshi fàng zài bāo li le.}}

{{把手机别忘了！|Bǎ shǒujī bié wàng le!}}
practice.why: {{别|bié}}, {{不|bù}} and {{没|méi}} go before {{把|bǎ}}.

lessons.title: Say what happened to you
lessons.summary: “My wallet's been stolen”, “I got soaked in the rain”, “My brother ate all the cake”: say what happened to someone or something.
lessons.topic: {{被|bèi}} (+ who) + verb + what came of it: {{我的钱包被偷了|wǒ de qiánbāo bèi tōu le}}; {{让|ràng}} in speech

goal.r: Wǒ de qiánbāo bèi tōu le!

dialog.r: Zěnme le? Nǐ zěnme bù gāoxìng?
dialog.tr: What's wrong? Why the long face?

dialog.r: Wǒ de shǒujī bèi tōu le!
dialog.tr: My phone's been stolen!

dialog.r: Á? Zài nǎr bèi tōu de?
dialog.tr: What? Where was it stolen?

dialog.t: 在地铁上。而且我还被雨淋湿了。
dialog.r: Zài dìtiě shang. Érqiě wǒ hái bèi yǔ línshī le.
dialog.tr: On the subway. And I got soaked in the rain, too.

dialog.r: Tài dǎoméi le!
dialog.tr: What bad luck!

blocks.means: a sentence that starts with the person or thing an action is done to: “The wallet was stolen.” Chinese makes it with {{被|bèi}}.

blocks.p: **{{被|bèi}}: what happened to it.** Start with the person or thing affected, then {{被|bèi}}, then the verb with what came of it: {{我的钱包被偷了。|Wǒ de qiánbāo bèi tōu le.}} “My wallet was stolen.” To say who did it, put them right after {{被|bèi}}: {{蛋糕被弟弟吃完了。|Dàngāo bèi dìdi chīwán le.}} “My little brother ate all the cake.”

table: My brother ate all the cake.
I got soaked in the rain.
He got told off by the teacher.

blocks.p: **Mostly for bad news.** Chinese uses {{被|bèi}} much less than English uses the passive, mostly when something went wrong: stolen, broken, caught, told off. For neutral facts, Chinese simply leaves out who did it: {{饭做好了。|Fàn zuòhǎo le.}} “Dinner's been made.” In everyday speech, {{让|ràng}} can replace {{被|bèi}} when you say who did it: {{我的自行车让人骑走了。|Wǒ de zìxíngchē ràng rén qízǒu le.}} “Someone's ridden off on my bike.”
Like {{把|bǎ}}, the verb after {{被|bèi}} needs something more ({{了|le}}, a result), and {{没|méi}} goes before {{被|bèi}}: {{我没被骗。|Wǒ méi bèi piàn.}} “I wasn't fooled.”

ex.r: Wǒ de qiánbāo bèi tōu le!

ex.tr: My little brother has eaten all the cake.
I got soaked in the rain.

ex.t: 他被公司派到上海去了。
ex.r: Tā bèi gōngsī pài dào Shànghǎi qù le.
ex.tr: His company has sent him to Shanghai.

ex.t: 我的自行车让人骑走了。
ex.r: Wǒ de zìxíngchē ràng rén qízǒu le.
ex.tr: Someone's ridden off on my bike.

blocks.tip: {{倒霉|dǎoméi}} “bad luck” is the natural reaction to most {{被|bèi}} stories: {{太倒霉了！|Tài dǎoméi le!}} “What bad luck!”

mistakes.why: After {{被|bèi}} the verb needs something more, here {{了|le}}: {{被偷了|bèi tōu le}}.
{{被|bèi}} is for things that happen to someone, often bad. To say who made something, use {{是…的|shì… de}}: {{这本书是我写的。|Zhè běn shū shì wǒ xiě de.}}
